Firefighters battle the inferno at Super Parts Limited on Hagley Park Road on Thursday. (Photo: Garfield Robinson) 


BY JASON CROSS Observer staff reporter crossj@jamaicaobserver.com 
 August 28, 2026




 Courage under fire 

Employees, taxi driver rush to save stock, cars in Superior Parts inferno 






Employees of Superior Parts Limited and a taxi driver battled to save millions of dollars worth of motorcycles and cars on Thursday as a raging fire tore through the company on Hagley Park Road in St Andrew, while firefighters were hampered by a lack of water amid the severe drought that has triggered water restrictions in sections of the island.

Although firefighters from seven stations in Kingston and St Catherine responded, the majority of the stock was destroyed in the midday inferno that sent thick black smoke into the air and created traffic snarls on Hagley Park Road and adjoining thoroughfares.

In the midst of the chaos and destruction, 71-year-old Leroy Terlon used a forklift to remove numerous wooden boxes from the premises and placed them on the road.

“I had to put out the energy and the effort to get certain things saved. I have been here for 20 years and I helped to build the company to where it is now, with labour and loyalty. This event shouldn’t have happened,” Terlon told the Jamaica Observer as he sipped a cold beer at a nearby gas station following his heroics.

He said he was cooling off after his exposure to the intense heat.

“This hurts me. This company is like mine. If I talk about it, tears will come to my eyes. I have been there for so long. It hurts me. I don’t have liquid cash in the business, but I have years of service,” he added as he received congratulatory messages from friends for his bravery.

Other employees also rushed to move stock from the building, while taxi operator Kemal Dunn used his car to tow motor vehicles from a car mart adjoining the burning property.

“I just saw it and said I had to help. I knew it would spread because Superior has a lot of boxes,” he told the Observer.

“I was just driving past. My uncle owns a car dealership up the road. This car dealership just started. For a trying man, I decided to just assist him as best as I could,” Dunn explained.

“Only one car got damaged out of more than 30 that were there. I helped them rescue a good 20 of them. I used my car to pull out some. We used a wire to jump-start others because they were parked for a good while and they had no power to start. I am glad I helped them to minimise the loss.

“I was just watching the electric wire. The fire, you just have to know how to stay a good distance because you are going to feel the heat. The wires were sparking and gashing.”

“I love to help a person and he can pass it on to a next person. I am not going to take my phone and video when I can help,” he added, taking an apparent jab at the many onlookers who stood recording the fire with their cellphones.

Dunn said he banged on the windows of neighbouring houses to ensure that no humans were inside.

“All of these things are material things that can be replaced. A lot of people won’t have a job tomorrow, but they still have life,” Dunn reasoned.

As the fire raged, people in a number of adjoining residential and commercial premises moved out as many supplies and furniture before the flames spread.

One Superior Parts employee, who wished to remain anonymous, speculated that welding sparked the blaze.

“There was welding going on around the back. The fire started around that side. Nobody is allowed to smoke on property, so we believe it started with the welding. We don’t see any other way the fire could have started,” the worker said.

Amid the devastation wrought by the fire, police were kept on their toes by onlookers who wanted to get close-up shots to post on social media. Cops were heard repeatedly telling them to remove from the area for their safety.

Other onlookers were heard venting that the motorbikes were being destroyed and the police did not allow them to go in and grab one for themselves.

Throughout the ordeal, power lines caught fire, sending sparks flying and forcing people to take cover. At the same time, numerous loud explosions were heard coming from the premises.

Three firefighters were reportedly injured during their attempt to put the blaze out.

The Observer was told that the Jamaica Fire Brigade had received a call alerting it to the fire at 12:08 pm. Units from Trench Town initially responded, but according to a firefighter who requested anonymity because he was not authorised to speak to the media, the magnitude of the fire was so great that units had to be requested from other stations.

“There were units from York Park, Half-Way-Tree, Rollington Town, Port Royal, Stony Hill, Portmore, and Spanish Town,” the firefighter said, while pointing to the difficulty they experienced accessing water at the scene.

“The water challenges were expected because of the drought conditions. A lot of the hydrants have no water or low water pressure and it was a massive fire,” he added.

Up to 6:00 pm, the fire had not been fully extinguished.

CLARKE... I believe the success of any business should also be measured by the opportunities it creates for others to rise, empowering generations and strengthening communities 


August 28, 2026




 Sandals Foundation head Heidi Clarke honoured with 2026 Skift IDEA Trailblazer Award 







IN recognition of her far-reaching impact, Sandals Foundation Executive Director Heidi Clarke has been selected to receive the prestigious ‘Trailblazer Award: Women Shaping the Future of Travel,’ as part of the 2026 Skift IDEA Awards. 

The Skift IDEA Awards are the travel industry’s way of recognising excellence in design, creativity, and innovation with winners being a beacon of where the industry is heading.

Presented in partnership with Women Leading Travel, the Trailblazer Award honours a woman whose career demonstrates exceptional leadership, resilience, and influence in shaping the future of travel.

Clarke, who heads the philanthropic arm of Sandals and Beaches resorts, has harnessed the power of tourism to strengthen communities and expand opportunity across the Caribbean.

Sandals Foundation Executive Director Heidi Clarke in her element with one of the many children who benefit from the work of the foundation.

Since the launch of the not-for-profit Sandals Foundation in 2009, Clarke has led initiatives that improve lives across the Caribbean, with a focus on education, community development, and environmental conservation in the nine islands where Sandals and Beaches resorts operate.

Under her care, the foundation has touched more than 1.8 million lives, supporting more than 2,600 schools, close to 200 large-scale conservation initiatives, and mobilising more than 32,500 volunteers across the region, among other extraordinary projects.

“It is truly an honour to be recognised, and I am immensely proud of what our team, together with our incredible partners, has made possible,” said Clarke.

“I believe the success of any business should also be measured by the opportunities it creates for others to rise, empowering generations and strengthening communities. Tourism has an extraordinary footprint, and when we harness that reach with purpose it can be a tremendous force for positive change across our Caribbean region,” added Clarke.

Her work has championed tourism as a force for positive, lasting change, bringing together communities, governments, non-profit organisations, businesses and travellers to address local needs and strengthen the destinations that sustain the industry.

Born and raised in Jamaica, she has spent nearly two decades developing programs that strengthen communities, expand economic opportunity and advance environmental stewardship throughout the Caribbean.

“Heidi is a true champion for the Caribbean and has dedicated her career to creating opportunities for its people and building a stronger future for the region,” said Adam Stewart, executive chairman of Sandals and Beaches Resorts and president of Sandals Foundation. “She leads with tremendous heart and purpose, and with an unwavering belief in the potential of our Caribbean communities. Her work through the Sandals Foundation is at the heart of who we are at Sandals Resorts and Beaches Resorts, and reflects our deep and enduring commitment to the region we call home. This recognition is incredibly well-deserved, and we could not be prouder of Heidi and the contributions she continues to make,” added Stewart.

The Skift IDEA Awards are now in their eighth year. The 2026 winners were evaluated through an initial review by the Skift Editorial Team, followed by an independent judging panel of travel and business leaders representing top hospitality organisations.

2025 JUNO nominee Skystar. 

 Entertainment 

Kevin Jackson 
 August 28, 2026




 Dancehall gets recognition from the JUNO Awards 







AHEAD of the 2027 staging of the JUNO Awards, Canada’s equivalent to the Grammys, the Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) has introduced a series of category and eligibility updates.

These updates, according to CARAS in a press release shared with the Jamaica Observer, are designed to better reflect Canada’s music community and to provide clear, meaningful pathways for artistes to have their work recognised.

The category Reggae Recording of the Year has been renamed Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year. The reggae category was first instituted in 1985 as Best Reggae/Calypso Recording. For the 1994 staging, the category was renamed Best Reggae Recording, with the name Reggae Recording of the Year coming into effect in 2003.

Canada-based dancehall artiste Phenique is pleased with the evolution of the JUNO Awards.

ANTHONY… the inclusion of dancehall in the JUNO Awards’ Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year category is a significant and long overdue step forward for our community.

“I’m excited to see the JUNO Awards continuing to evolve and recognise the diversity within today’s music. I think these changes create more opportunities for artists across different genres to have their work recogniSed and celebrated. It’s definitely a positive step forward,” Phenique told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

Recording artiste, broadcaster and curator of the weekly Reggae North Canadian Reggae/Dancehall Top 20 chart, Tony Anthony, believes that the inclusion of dancehall is long overdue.

“The inclusion of Dancehall in the JUNO Awards’ Reggae/Dancehall Recording of the Year category is a significant and long-overdue step forward for our community. Industry professionals and supporters within the reggae and Dancehall community have advocated for Dancehall to be properly recognised on one of Canada’s biggest music stages. This announcement is not just a change in the name of a category—it is an acknowledgment of the cultural impact, creativity and contribution that Dancehall has made to Canadian music and to the broader music industry. This is an important milestone, but also a reminder that our community must continue to advocate for both genres and ensure that its artists receive the respect, visibility and opportunities that come with being recognized as a vital part of Canada’s music industry,” Tony Anthony disclosed.

2025 JUNO nominee dancehall artiste Skystar, who is originally from the Kingston 20 area, sees the revamping of the reggae category to include dancehall as a step forward.

“I’m excited to see the JUNOS expanding the conversation to officially recognise dancehall. Reggae is deeply rooted in Jamaican culture, but Dancehall has grown into a powerful global movement that continues to influence music, fashion, language and youth culture around the world,” he noted. “For artists like myself who represent the next generation of Jamaican music here in Canada, this recognition matters. It tells us that the sound, culture and evolution of our music are being seen and valued. I believe this is a great step forward, and I hope we continue creating space for the many different sounds and generations that make Reggae and Dancehall so powerful. Respect to the JUNOS for recognising the culture.”

Canada-based dancehall artiste Phenique.

However, Carrie Mullings, former chair of the Reggae Committee for the JUNO Awards, says dancehall music was always submitted for consideration.

“During my time with the JUNO’s (17 years, 12 as a chair) the category already consisted of dancehall submissions when you read the category description. As much as it is nice for the word Dancehall to be included in the category title it was never excluded. I feel these small steps are good but the bigger conversation in my opinion is the fact that an album body of work and a single can be submitted in the same category. We should be addressing the reason the category has not been split into 2, 1 for Reggae/Dancehall Recording of The Year (for single submissions) and 1 for Reggae/Dancehall Album/EP of the Year. As our music grows, collectively we should express our needs for expansion and recognition. Reggae/dancehall has walked the JUNO Red Carpet since 1985, please acknowledge our culture’s growth and award it accordingly,” said Mullings.

Other category changes for the 2027 JUNO Awards include:

Rap: Melodic Rap Recording of the Year and Rap Recording of the Year will replace Rap Album/EP of the Year and Rap Single of the Year.

MULLINGS…I feel these small steps are good but the bigger conversation, in my opinion, is the fact that an album body of work and a single can be submitted in the same category.

Electronic/Dance: Electronic/Dance Single of the Year and Electronic/Dance Album/EP of the Year will replace Electronic Album of the Year and Dance Recording of the Year.

Contemporary Christian/Gospel: Contemporary Christian/Gospel Recording of the Year will replace Contemporary Christian/Gospel Album of the Year, with singles, EPs and albums now eligible.

The submission for awards and songs for consideration for the 2027 staging of the JUNO Awards will open on September 21 with November 5 being the final submission date.

The 56th annual JUNO Awards will be broadcast live from Canada Life Centre in Winnipeg, Manitoba, on Sunday, April 4, 2027. JUNO Week runs from April 1 to 4, 2027.

Nation’s Choice chief executive Donald McDonald shows pallets of frozen products inside the company’s Clarendon cold-storage facility, part of a roughly $1-billion investment aimed at expanding capacity for the hospitality sector. 

 Business, Caribbean Business Report (CBR) 

BY DASHAN HENDRICKS Business content manager hendricksd@jamaicaobserver.com 
 August 28, 2026




 Nation’s Choice makes $1-billion hotel bet 

Clarendon food company targets regional exports as it expands cold storage and manufacturing 






Nations Choice has invested about $1 billion in new cold storage capacity as the Jamaican food company positions itself for increased demand from the hotel sector while preparing to export locally manufactured products across the Caribbean.

Guyana is expected to be the first export market early next year, Chief Executive Officer Donald McDonald said, with Barbados, St Lucia and the Cayman Islands also among the countries being targeted.

The Clarendon-based company imports and distributes frozen and chilled seafood, meats, poultry and vegetables, but has been steadily increasing manufacturing as it builds the Nations Choice name into a consumer brand.

“We are preparing ourselves now to start exporting from Jamaica some of the products that we manufacture,” McDonald told the Jamaica Observer in an interview on Wednesday. “We have gone into some markets, done some market surveys, and there is a lot of interest in some of the products that we do manufacture.”

The planned exports would include burgers, bacon, ham and pickled products made in Jamaica. Nations Choice already moves some branded products into other Caribbean countries but McDonald said those goods are produced or packaged outside Jamaica. That activity accounts for only about one to two per cent of the company’s business.

Nations Choice CEO Donald McDonald shows the Jamaica Observer the company’s new cold-storage facility in Clarendon, part of a roughly $1-billion investment aimed at expanding capacity for the hospitality sector.

Nations Choice has invested an estimated $4 billion since starting in 2011 with two containers and five products, McDonald said. The company now employs more than 300 people and handles about 200 stock-keeping units.

The larger cold storage facility represents an investment of about $1 billion and can hold about four million kilogrammes of product. A separate picking room, which is not included in that investment, has capacity for about 1,500 pallets. The operation runs around the clock.

McDonald said the investment was made with Jamaica’s expanding hotel pipeline in mind. Hospitality already accounts for about 20 per cent of Nations Choice’s business, with the remaining 80 per cent coming from the wider local market, including institutions and consumers.

He expects between 8,000 and 9,000 hotel rooms to come on stream over the next two years, which he believes will create additional demand for food suppliers.

Government filings reported in July identified 13 hotel projects facilitated by Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro), that are expected to add 8,943 rooms, although the developments have varying completion timelines and some have been delayed.

“I think that presents a great opportunity for growth in servicing that sector,” McDonald said. “That is why we’re interested in building this new cold storage, positioning ourselves to be able to service the hospitality sector.”

Workers package burgers at Nations Choice’s Clarendon operation, where the company produces about 29,000 burger patties each week.

The bet on hotels comes while that part of Nations Choice’s business is still recovering from Hurricane Melissa. McDonald estimated that the company’s hospitality business was down about 30 per cent in November and December as a number of properties closed, particularly in western Jamaica.

The impact was partly offset in the months that followed as hotels that remained open operated at high occupancy because fewer rooms were available. Nations Choice also supplied protein and frozen vegetables to Central Kitchen during its hot meal operations following the hurricane.

McDonald said the company has not yet fully re-established its hotel business because some properties remain closed while others are only now reopening.

Nations Choice is also putting more weight behind products it makes itself. Manufacturing began in 2017 with pig tail and mackerel and has since expanded to burgers, ham, bacon and other processed foods.

McDonald said the company now produces about 29,000 burger patties each week, while locally manufactured products account for roughly 15 per cent of what it distributes.

A sample of Nations Choice chicken bacon, a new locally manufactured product the company plans to introduce in early September.

Over the past three years Nations Choice has also increased the number of products sold under its own brand in supermarkets, moving beyond its traditional business-to-business model supplying hotels, restaurants, wholesalers and institutions such as schools, hospitals and prisons.

Its locally manufactured range includes curried goat and jerk pork burgers, with chicken bacon due to be added in early September.

“We are launching a chicken bacon,” McDonald said.

Those locally made products are also being lined up for the regional push. Nations Choice already supplies Guyana with goods sourced from other jurisdictions, McDonald said, but is now preparing to supply the market with products manufactured in Jamaica.

“I would say we have broken in already because we are already moving products there from other jurisdictions,” he said. “It is just a matter of moving products now from Jamaica there, which is what we are preparing ourselves to start doing.”

Donald McDonald, chief executive officer of Nations Choice, says the company is preparing to export Jamaican-made products into regional markets while expanding its manufacturing operations.

news.title: Trump abandons June MoU terms, complicating diplomatic efforts to reopen Strait of Hormuz - WSJ
news.text: US President Donald Trump told its mediators and regional partners that it is uninterested in returning to the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding outlined in June, The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday.The report noted that the administration's stubborn refusal to go back to the terms it reached with Iran earlier this summer has significantly complicated the diplomatic process of restarting negotiations.After Iran started attacking ships in the strait in an attempt to regain control, Trump began his “Economic D-Day” campaign on Iran, which the White House is calling Operation Economic Outcast.In his announcement, Trump claimed that the campaign would bring “economic Warfare and Isolation on an unprecedented scale,” though he provided few other details.Trump wants to move past MoU, Iran warns of attacks on HormuzSources familiar with the matter told the WSJ that Trump is no longer interested in the MoU, which has been heavily criticized as a deal that is too soft on Iran.“As the president said, there are no talks or conversations going on, or scheduled, with the Islamic Republic of Iran,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said, as reported by the WSJ.“The naval blockade remains in full force and effect, and Operation Economic Outcast is underway to sever every remaining economic lifeline sustaining the regime.”The report indicated that Iranian hardliners' positions will make it difficult for Trump to achieve a foreign policy win, which he has repeatedly pushed for.Regime hardliners have repeatedly derailed talks by insisting that the US recognize Iranian authority over the strait and move its warships out of the area.Iranian officials have warned the US administration against any departure from the June MoU.The administration “should know that no proposal outside the framework of understanding will be accepted,” senior legislator Mohammad Rashidi told Iranian state news outlet Icana, as quoted by the WSJ.Several regional mediators have tried to sway Iran's demands, but have seen little progress. Sources told the WSJ that the sharpening demands leave mediators without a clear way to restart talks.Oman, Qatar meet with Iranian officials to negotiateRepresentatives from Pakistan and Oman traveled to Iran earlier this week with varying results. Sources told the WSJ that Pakistani army chief Asim Munir left Tehran with little to show for his efforts. Omani Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Al Busaidi also traveled to Tehran this past week, and the two sides reportedly hammered out an agreement that would lead to talks to reopen Hormuz. The administration reportedly has been upset at Oman, believing that Muscat gave away too much to Tehran.While Iran has claimed the meeting resulted in a deal, Oman has yet to comment on the matter.Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman al-Thani also reportedly recently traveled to Iran to meet with the country's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi.A joint statement released after the talks said that the pair discussed how to avoid regional escalation and begin the groundwork for talks.On Wednesday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said Hormuz would not reopen until the US returns to the June MoU terms, which included an end to the US blockade.“If the United States stops obstructing and returns to the memorandum of understanding, we can open the Strait of Hormuz within the framework of the agreement reached,” Revolutionary Guard spokesman Brig. Gen. Hossein Mohebbi told state media.“Our conditions must be accepted by the United States.”Mohebbi also vowed heavy blows to US vital interests and energy chokepoints if Iran's infrastructure is threatened, Press TV reported.Last week, Iran announced that it shifted its policy from defensive to "fully offensive" due to the deadlock in efforts to agree on a permanent end to the war. "Iranian entities must be prepared to escalate tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region, as Iran will be ready to make decisions and take action on difficult decisions," an Iranian official told Reuters, adding that Tehran would conduct a "timely and precise" military attack to break the US naval blockade if diplomacy failed.Reuters contributed to this report.

 August 28, 2026




 MORE WITH LESS 

ISSA president looks to competitive schoolboy football season despite sponsorship fall-off 






DESPITE ISSA working with one of its smallest sponsorship budgets for schoolboy football in recent times, President Keith Wellington believes this season could be one of the best yet, thanks to a revamped structure across the various competitions. 

The launch of the prestigious under-19 high school football season was held on Wednesday, with the daCosta Cup set to begin next Saturday while the Manning Cup kicks off four days later.

However ISSA will execute the competitions with less sponsorship dollars this year, which Wellington says is down to a little over $40 million.

Long-time sponsor Wisynco, which supported the competition for more than a decade through its various brands, has not returned this year after investing $37.3 million in last year’s season. Bert’s Auto Parts has also not returned after coming on board in 2025.

Jusanna Staple (white shirt), WATA brand co-ordinator, and ISSA President Keith Wellington present the winning trophy to Excelsior High team members after they defeated Jamaica College 2-0 in the Manning Cup final at the National Stadium on December 19, 2025. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

KFC; Kirk Distributors through its brands Kendel and Cetamol; and Charles Chocolate, through its brand Ping Pong, have remained on board while Happy Ice has joined as a new sponsor, just weeks after former Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) Operations Manager Omar McFarlane was named CEO.

While grateful for the current partnerships Wellington says fan support will be crucial this season to help offset the sponsorship shortfall.

“It has and will have a significant impact on schoolboy football in terms of what we are hoping to do. That is why it is even more important that the fans come out and support the competition,” he said. “This is their thing; it’s the fans’ thing. They want to see schoolboy football each year, they want to see their schools participate, and their support in coming and paying $500 at the gate, those little contributions will help to support their schools.”

“We provide all the schools with playing gear, we provide the referee fees for everybody, and obviously we have to find venues when it comes to the latter stages of the competition so we need the support of the general public.”

(From left) ISSA President Keith Wellington, St Elizabeth Technical Head Coach Omar Wedderburn, KFC Brand Manager Andrei Roper, Kendel/Cetamol Business Development Manager Tynielle Chambers-Barnett and Calabar head Coach Kemar Ricketts are locked in discussion during the schoolboy football launch at CVM TV headquarters on Wednesday.

This season will be one of the most unique in the near-120-year history of schoolboy football. The top 15 teams from both the Manning Cup and DaCosta Cup have earned byes into the second round, with nine teams from the Manning Cup first round and 21 from the daCosta Cup first round advancing to join them.

Wellington says this could lead to a more competitive season compared to previous years.

“We are hoping that the first round — where the teams we believe are more equally matched — will be a lot more competitive and the best teams will advance. And they advance having played [5, 6, 7 games already] to compete against the more established programmes who may have played a lot more practice matches.”

The formats of the knockout competitions, the urban area Walker Cup, and the rural area Ben Francis Cup have also changed, with the top 32 teams now competing. For the past seven years the semi-finalists of the Manning and daCosta Cup were unable to compete.

The all-island knockout tournament, the Champions Cup, will have its format decided during the season.

St Elizabeth Technical football players celebrate with fans after the team’s penalty shoot-out victory over Glenmuir High in the ISSA daCosta Cup final at the National Stadium on December 20, 2025. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

“We are happy that most persons are comfortable with the changes and are happy to see the changes. What we need to do now is to ensure that we execute properly and that we get the support, not just from the teams involved but from the supporting cast — the students, the general public, and corporate Jamaica, to ensure that we have a successful season,” said Wellington.

Excelsior High will look to defend their Manning Cup title while St Elizabeth Technical (STETHS) will look to retain their daCosta Cup title. Clarendon College are the only team from either competition to have successfully defended their title since 2018.

Manning Cup seeded teams: Excelsior, Jamaica College, St Catherine, Wolmer’s Boys’, Campion College, Charlie Smith, Calabar, St Jago, STATHS, Kingston College, Tivoli Gardens, St George’s College, Eltham, Mona, Vauxhall.

daCosta Cup seeded teams: STETHS, Glenmuir, Clarendon College, Dinthill Technical, Cornwall College, Kemps Hill, Maggotty High, Old Harbour, Garvey Maceo, McGrath, Ocho Rios, Christiana, Manchester, Manning’s, William Knibb

The 2027 BYD ATTO 8 was launched over two days — Saturday, August 22 at Kingston Polo Club and Sunday, August 23, with a test drive day at the Police Officers’ Club, St Andrew. 


BY RORY DALEY Observer writer editorial@jamaiaobserver.com 
 August 28, 2026




 BYD welcomes ATTO 8 







BYD JAMAICA, the arm of ATL Automotive Group responsible for the BYD line of new energy vehicles, rolled out the red carpet for the latest addition to its model line-up, the ATTO 8, with two days of activities this month.

“It’s a dream come true to have the ATTO 8 on Jamaican shores,” Sloane Jackson, head of business, BYD Jamaica, told the Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

The vehicle was launched on Saturday, August 22, at Kingston Polo Club with the opportunity to test-drive it the following day, Sunday, August 23, at Police Officers’ Club, St Andrew.

Jackson explained that the ATTO 8 was not a given, and that it was a process to bring it to market from China, having seen it last April at Auto Shanghai 2025. He and his team were privy to a special and private unveiling of the vehicle.

The interior of the ATTO 8 carries an abundance of technology, luxury features, and premium build quality.

“One of the things they showed us that wasn’t unveiled at the show, but unveiled to us as the BYD team, was the new Tang. What they told us was that it would be called the Sealion 8 in some markets, and the ATTO 8 in our region, available as a full EV and as a hybrid. We were initially told that we might get it,” Jackson said.

After the revelation that it would be available in right-hand drive, as it was going to be sold in the Australian and South African markets, Jackson felt it would be a great fit for the Caribbean region and his Jamaica portfolio.

The ATTO 8 is a mid-sized SUV, using BYD’s hybrid technology. Currently, it is only available in one trim level, DM-p, which makes it an all-wheel-drive plug-in hybrid vehicle. The drivetrain is similar to the BYD Shark pickup. Under the bonnet of the ATTO 8 is a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder engine. The petrol engine is paired with two electric motors — front and rear — for a total power output of 536bhp. The 35.6kWh battery is rated to deliver 152km of pure electric range, with a combined range up to 1,400km. It can be charged externally at 11kWh for AC, and DC fast-charged at 72kWh using the CCS2 port. The ATTO 8 can also do Vehicle-to-Load to run attached electrical devices.

On the performance front, 100kph can be reached in under five seconds, with a top speed of 200kph.

The ATTO 8 uses a hybrid drivetrain pairing a 1.5-litre turbocharged four-cylinder engine with two electric motors — front and rear — for a total power output of 536bhp.

Beyond its speed and range as a seven-seat SUV, the ATTO 8 is packed with the technology expected from BYD. There’s wireless charging and USB ports throughout a spacious cabin that features integrated multi-colour ambient lighting, premium materials, double-layer glass for the front doors, and a 21-speaker sound system.

For family use, there is a maximum 1,960-litres of cargo capacity, powered seating — including the ability to control the front passenger from the second row, and even amenities such as a massage function for the second row. There are driver aids for safety and convenience, while the BYD infotainment offers up its usual wide range of interactivity.

Jackson said that the sales numbers of the ATTO 8, to date, have justified its addition to the showroom floor, as it comes at a time when rising fuel prices are driving the automotive consumer’s buying habits, gaining BYD’s line-up of electric vehicles and hybrids even more attention. This was a sentiment mirrored by Mark Dommisse, managing director, ATL Automotive Group.

“We are exceptionally lucky to host this brand in our portfolio. I would say that BYD is the heavyweight champion of the Chinese brands around the world, and that has definitely shown today. When we took on the brand two years ago, I think there was a lot of curiosity from the general public and a lot of questions. Every time the name BYD was asked, it was always with a question mark; nowadays it’s a mainstay brand that everybody knows. It’s trendy, it’s sexy, and they’re bringing out new products left, right, and centre. We’re certainly very happy with the sales volume. We’re very happy with the return on investment, and we’re honoured to hold the brand,” he said.

With three rows of seating the ATTO 8 has a multitude of cargo configurations to handle luggage.

Beyond the launch, guests were given free rein to examine the ATTO 8’s features to the fullest, while being treated to food, drink, and activities, including creating a signature car fragrance.

The 2027 ATTO 8 DM-p is now available from BYD Jamaica at $15 million, with the EV model expected to arrive next year.

“All that is available to us in right-hand drive is the hybrid. The EV model should be coming in the middle of 2028, which will have the most powerful single electric motor ever built, with the option of 1,000 bhp,” said Jackson.

From left: Mark Dommisse, managing director,ATL Automotive Group; Kellise Wong, group marketing manager, ATL Automotive Group; Stephen Hector, group strategic marketing and digital director; Theresa Higgins-Edwards, senior marketing manager, BYD Jamaica; and Sloane Jackson, head of business, BYD Jamaica, at the August 22 launch of the BYD ATTO 8.

The ATTO 8 launch saw BYD partners in attendance from around the Caribbean.

Ingrid Henry | Observer Writer 
 August 28, 2026




 Sole survivor stitches dad’s legacy into every shoe 







ANNOTTO BAY, St Mary — Step inside Third World Home of Footwork on this town’s main street and you will hear it before you see it: the tap-tap of a hammer on leather, the whirr of a sewing machine, with the faint smell of glue and shoe polish hanging in the air.

Behind the counter is 33-year-old Ria Anderson working on a pair of shoes. Her hands move with the same confidence she saw in her father Lloyd during the more than three decades he manned the store.

When Lloyd opened the doors to Third World Home of Footwork back in 1981, handmade shoes were not a luxury — they were a necessity. He quickly became the one people in Annotto Bay and other areas of the parish called when all hope seemed lost.

“His craftsmanship brought him many customers from across the island and overseas,” Ria recalls, pride in her voice.

“He was known to repair anything that is leather — from handbags to shoes — that owners thought would be unrepairable. During that time the demand for his handmade shoes was [very high],” she told the Jamaica Observer.

Nine years ago her father migrated and went into retirement. Many thought that was the end of Third World Home of Footwear but Ria refused to let the tools of his trade go cold.

“I grew up watching my father repairing and making shoes and sometimes I would do a little sewing on them. With that, I learned the trade that continues to put food on my table,” she told the Observer.

Today she is one of the few young women in Jamaica still practising the skill her father mastered. She takes pleasure in cutting, stitching, resoling and breathing new life into footwear that most would throw away.

Over the years Ria has seen the market evolve and watched as imported brands, often cheaper then her handmade wares, flooded the shelves. She is unbothered, confident the quality of her work will always lure clients to her store.

“They buy these shoes that are made from cheap and poor materials and then they want it fixed when it gets damaged. It comes right back to me and it is done better than before,” said Ria.

A custom-made pair of shoes crafted inside her shop starts at $10,000. Not cheap, but she argues it is an investment.

“These will last you for years, and not months, as the materials used are genuine leather and not a knock off. I am filling a gap with quality, repair, and the kind of personal service you [often] cannot get, [even] in a high-end store,” Ria said.

With only one apprentice she worries that when she retires there will be no one to continue the trade, but for as long as possible she is determined to keep not only her father’s name alive but the craft he loved dearly.

“This shop is his name, the trade that supported his family. This is his legacy,” she said as she ran her hand over a freshly polished shoe.

For Ria as long as people need shoes that last, she will be there.

BY JEROME WILLIAMS Observer staff reporter williamsj@jamaicaobserver.com 
 August 28, 2026




 Williams: Gov’t made ‘very good offer’ to teachers; awaits JTA response 







WITH teachers turning their backs on the Government’s latest wage proposal, Finance Minister Fayval Williams says the Administration believes it put forward a “very good offer” and is now awaiting further communication from the Jamaica Teachers’ Association (JTA) on its position and the way forward.

Williams was responding a Jamaica Observer query Thursday after the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service signed a wage negotiation agreement with the Jamaica Confederation of Trade Unions (JCTU), marking a significant development in the wider public sector wage negotiations.

But while the Government has reached a tentative wage settlement with the JCTU, the dispute with the JTA remains unresolved, with Williams telling the Observer that the Administration is awaiting word from the teachers’ union as to how it wants the negotiations to proceed.

The JTA rejected the Government’s latest wage offer at its 62nd annual conference in Trelawny on August 18. Of the 213 votes cast by delegates, 155 were against the offer, 54 were in favour, and four were rejected.

Newly elected JTA President LaSonja Harrison subsequently said the union would formally notify the Ministry of Finance and the Public Service of the outcome, and request the earliest possible date for negotiations to resume.

A week after the JTA rejected the proposal, Williams acknowledged the union’s dissatisfaction but said the Government would wait to see what position the association takes when it comes back to the ministry.

“We put forward what we felt to be a very good offer to the JTA. At their most recent conference you heard the incoming president speak. There is nothing I can add to that until we hear back from them, whether in writing or in a meeting, as to what their thoughts are [and] what the go-forward is,” she told the Observer.

“They have indicated that they are not satisfied, and they listed some of the items. So, at this point, we can only wait and see what their posture is when they come back,” she added.

The JTA’s rejection was driven by concerns that extended beyond the basic salary component of the Government’s proposal. Harrison said delegates had raised several outstanding issues during their deliberations, including the remote inducement allowance, uniform package, protective clothing, and graduate allowance.

On the uniform package, Harrison pointed to what she described as a significant disparity between the provisions for teachers and the existing public sector uniform policy.

“The Government of Jamaica has three or four levels in the uniform policy, and the smallest remuneration package is $135,000, yet the Government has offered the teachers not one of the four categories, but $38,500,” Harrison said.

She argued that the proposed amount does not allow teachers to fit into the categories established under the policy.

 Cricket, Sports 

Ruddy Allen | Sports Writer 
 August 28, 2026




 Lawes hails CPL as ultimate battleground for career development 







VITEL Lawes believes the Caribbean Premier League (CPL) is the perfect classroom for young West Indies white-ball cricketers, and the 19-year-old left-arm wrist spinner is determined to use the lessons to build his senior career across all three formats of the game.

Jamaica Kingsmen bowler Lawes said he is enjoying his first taste of CPL cricket and that the exposure has been invaluable.

“I mean, the CPL is the biggest party in sport, you know. It’s a place where you can come and learn more about the skills in white-ball cricket, get exposed to different things, different types of batsmen.

“It’s a good learning experience, so it’s just for me to take the learnings and go back to the drawing board after the CPL and do the necessary work,” Lawes told the Jamaica Observer.

Lawes, who also debuted for the West Indies senior team recently, said he is not thinking short term.

“It’s been a good experience, you know, playing for West Indies at a very young age. People think it adds a lot of pressure on you but I don’t really think about it; I just go there and do what I do best, you know, enjoy the game.

“I want a long-term career, you know. I want to play all three formats of the game, but in order to do that I have to put in the work — and I think I’m willing to do that,” he explained.

He credited much of his progress to West Indies spin coach, Nikita Miller.

“I’ve just been doing my work with Nikita Miller on the side. I just follow instructions of what I’ve been given. I’ve just been following what I’ve been told, and I’ve been stringing my balls.

LAWES… it’s just for me to continue doing what I’ve been doing (Photo: ICC Media)

“I think I’m getting better. I mean, the results speak for themselves in ODI [One-Day International] cricket so it’s just for me to continue doing what I’ve been doing,” Lawes said.

Lawes said that the leg-spin journey started in his living room.

“I started at a very young age watching the same CPL, watching the Jamaica Tallawahs was playing, and they had Adam Zampa. That’s how I started bowling spin in the first place. I don’t know what to tell you about my bowling, to be honest, I just do what I do best. I just spin the ball, that’s all I do,” he said.

He didn’t realise it was serious until later.

“Never knowing what I was doing was real until later, about 11 years old, and people took me in and tried to teach me the sport. So that’s how it basically started,” he noted.

A St Jago High School graduate, Lawes says his support system has been crucial. His mother, Ilyn Henry-Campbell, is his biggest fan.

“She’s made a lot of sacrifices for me growing up so it’s the least I can do for her to make her proud. She used to listen to cricket at a young age. She used to buy battery for the radio to listen to cricket so I think she’ll be very proud of her son to be playing for the West Indies at this time,” he said.

And his schoolmates never doubted him.

“I mean, they always told me I will do well. They always believed in me. Nothing’s changed between us. We’ve still been normal friends,” he said.

 News, Western 

Anthony Lewis | Observer Writer 
 August 28, 2026




 Don’t lock students out 

Education ministry again appeals to school officials 






ROSE HALL, St James — As students prepare for the new academic starting next month, parliamentary secretary in the Ministry of Education, Senator Marlon Morgan is reminding school administrators not to lock students out for breaches of uniform and grooming standards.

“I just want to remind each school leader of the Government’s directive: If a child presents at school, presents for instruction, and is in some way in violation of a school rule — for example, the grooming standards or the uniform — do not have the student locked out of the school,” stated Morgan.

He was addressing the Region 4 Principals’ Leadership Conference and Appreciation Luncheon 2026, held at Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James on Thursday.

“The direction from the ministry is for the child to be admitted and appropriate punishment or remedy administered within the context of the school,” stated Morgan as he highlighted the responsibilities of school administrators.

“We have an obligation to attend to and cater to the well-being of our children, and we do not want them to come into harm’s way or be susceptible to the vagaries of the elements outside of the school gate,” he stressed.

“If they are in violation of the school rules in terms of uniform or whatever, ensure that you admit them. Whether you are going to place them in a particular space, whatever the arrangement or situation is, administer the discipline within the confines and context of the school,” urged the senator.

His reminder comes ahead of the much-anticipated roll-out of a National Student Dress and Grooming Policy.

Addressing the Jamaica Teachers’ Association 62nd annual conference in Trelawny last week, Education Minister Dr Dana Morris Dixon revealed that the new policy will require schools to have written grooming standards, clearly outline sanctions for breaches, apply rules consistently, and ensure that parents are fully informed. She did not provide a date by which it would be available.

August 28, 2026




 JN Money support brings tears of joy to laid-off mother 

10 PEP students buoyed by company’s ‘Support Their Start’ campaign 






TWO families in Montego Bay, St James, are among recipients welcoming timely relief from the financial pressures of the new school year through JN Money’s Support Their Start campaign.

The initiative is providing back-to-school assistance to 10 Primary Exit Profile (PEP) students as they prepare to transition to new schools this September.

For the mothers of two recipients in Montego Bay, preparing their children for the new school year was already a financial challenge, made more difficult by the economic impact of Hurricane Melissa last October.

Davia Wilson, mother of 12-year-old Ageia Reid who is transitioning from Anchovy Primary to Westwood High School, said the call informing her that she had been selected for the assistance came at a critical time.

The hurricane had disrupted her family’s circumstances, with the temporary closure of her workplace affecting her income and forcing her to dip into her savings to help prepare her daughter for her new boarding school.

When she received the news about the assistance she became so overwhelmed with emotion that she broke down in tears during the phone call.

“I personally didn’t know the expenses would have been so hectic and so much for the first year,” related Wilson.

“When I got the call it was like everything in my world just stopped. I was really excited because it just took off some of the weight that I am carrying,” added Wilson.

She said with normalcy at her workplace expected to return in December, she even visited Westwood High School to inform administrators of her circumstances and discuss her anticipated challenges for the upcoming term.

Davia Wilson cried tears of joy when she heard that her daughter,12-year-old Ageia Reid, who is transitioning from Anchovy Primary to Westwood High School, had been selected for assistance from JN Money.

“I had totally forgotten about the book list too, and the day I remembered about it was the same day I got the call — so I can put this money towards the books and other things to help prepare my daughter,” shared Wilson.

She said the assistance represents more than financial support for her daughter.

“My little girl has been through a lot. Anchovy was her fifth primary school, and to see her work hard to pass her PEP exams for her school of choice means so much to us. We really appreciate the assistance from JN Money, and to her this is like a reward for all the hard work that she has put in,” Wilson pointed out.

Meanwhile Feleisha Campbell-McKenzie — mother of 12-year-old Kaelen Anglin who is transitioning from Catherine Hall Primary and Infant School to Herbert Morrison Technical High School — said, “We are extremely grateful that JN Money thought it necessary to support our back-to-school preparation, and I am on top of the moon.”

Campbell-McKenzie said as a married mother of two, and with both children to consider for going back to school, the season gets more demanding every year.

She related that while her immediate family was spared from destruction caused by Hurricane Melissa, “We took in family members, extending our hands and our hearts where we could.”

She noted that the support from JN Money will help her purchase books, school uniforms, shoes and a school bag for her son.

She said the assistance has also reinforced for her son that others recognise his potential and are also invested in his success. “This has really motivated and encouraged him to continue doing well.”

Cedrica Reid, head of marketing and sales at JN Money, explained that supporting families and investing in the education of people remain important to the company, with the launch of the back-to-school campaign underscoring the organisation’s commitment to the communities it serves and the significant role remittances continue to play in Jamaica’s development.

August 28, 2026




 Rodri elated with Barca debut in win over Athletic Bilbao 







BARCELONA, Spain (AFP) — Raphinha and Fermin Lopez goals helped Spanish champions Barcelona beat Athletic Bilbao 2-0 on Thursday in La Liga to continue their perfect start to the season.

The Catalan giants eased to a solid victory over their Basque visitors in their first game of the season at the partially-rebuilt Camp Nou, with new arrival Rodri coming on for his Barca debut.

Raphinha rounded the goalkeeper and slid home in the 37th minute to give Barca the lead and Lopez netted after 82 minutes to secure the points, with the Catalans missing several chances for more goals and twice hitting the woodwork.

“Very happy to play my first game, happy with the victory. We’ve got two from two,” Rodri told DAZN.

“It’s important to keep building up rhythm and adapting to this great team. My first minutes and [I had] good feelings.”

Barca coach Hansi Flick made three changes to the team that thrashed Elche 5-0 last weekend, handing Anthony Gordon his first start for the club while bringing Pedri Gonzalez into midfield and picking Pau Cubarsi in defence.

The German kept Raphinha playing up front as a makeshift number nine, after the departures of Robert Lewandowski and Ferran Torres.

Barca have fruitlessly tried to pry Julian Alvarez away from Atletico Madrid, who will not negotiate with the Spanish champions for the Argentina forward.

However, Raphinha netted twice from his striker’s role against Elche and was on target again for Barca at Camp Nou, giving them a deserved lead at half-time.

“It doesn’t matter which position Rapha plays, as a captain he’s shown total commitment to this team, to this club,” Flick told reporters.

“You can see the supporters are connected with him and it’s really good.”

The Brazilian nodded against the post from Xavi Espart’s cross midway through the first half and Lamine Yamal’s follow-up effort was deflected wide, with Barca controlling the game.

Eventually, they took the lead when Pedri slipped Raphinha through on goal, with the Brazilian rounding Unai Simon and rolling home.

Teenage star Yamal should have doubled Barca’s lead before the interval but Simon made a fine save to deny him, while Gordon complained that he would have had an open goal if the Spain international had knocked the ball across to him.

Gordon arrowed a shot narrowly over early in the second half as Barcelona probed for a second goal.

Yamal, still not at his best level since suffering a hamstring injury in April, hit the crossbar with an effort from the edge of the box. Simon saved twice from Lopez, who netted a brace in the opener.

Flick sent on former Manchester City midfielder Rodri for his debut in midfield, leaving 10 Spaniards and Gordon on the pitch for Barca.

The champions were in the ascendency but Athletic threatened on a rare venture forward, with Oihan Sancet drilling against the post.

Barcelona eventually found their second after a mistake from Athletic defender Aymeric Laporte, clumsily nudging Barca substitute Karim Adeyemi’s cross past Simon, allowed for Lopez to tuck into an empty net.

Adeyemi should have netted a third late on when Yamal picked him out at the back post but Simon denied the German from point-blank range.

Yamal’s second-half performance was an improvement on a disappointing opening 45 minutes and his struggles against Elche, and Rodri said the forward is improving.

“Maybe Lamine came from a moment where he was a bit down and today we tried to help him get back up and saw his best version, even though he didn’t score,” added Rodri, Spain’s World Cup-winning captain.

“The goals will come because the talent is there.”

Athletic Bilbao have started their season with two defeats under new coach, Edin Terzic.

“I’m not a constant winner, I’m a constant trier,” said former Borussia Dortmund coach, Terzic.

“I’m fully of belief and trust when I see how we worked in these two games and in the training ground. Sooner or later we’ll get what we deserve and turn results in our favour.”

 Bouaddi needs time to settle at Man City, says Maresca 







MANCHESTER, United Kingdom (AFP) — Ayyoub Bouaddi is “ready to go” for his Manchester City debut at Crystal Palace on Friday, but Enzo Maresca called for patience with the most expensive teenager in Premier League history.

A star of Morocco’s run to the World Cup quarter-finals, the 18-year-old joined City on Wednesday for an initial 100 million euros (£85.6 million,US $117 million) from Lille.

City moved for Bouaddi after selling a trio of midfielders in Spain’s World Cup-winning captain Rodri, Tijjani Reijnders and Nico Gonzalez in recent weeks.

“We will see how long it is in terms of adaptation but for sure he is ready to go,” Maresca told his pre-match press conference on Thursday.

“He doesn’t look 18 — he looks older which is important but in this case we need to go slowly because he is young, came from a different country.

“No rush for him. For sure he will help us now and in the future. But he is just 18.

“It is my job and it’s the club’s job to manage him in the best way, don’t put pressure on him, he is young and he needs time.”

City’s exodus has seen Bernardo Silva and John Stones also depart in the wake of Pep Guardiola ending his trophy-laden decade as manager at the Etihad.

A move for Chelsea’s Enzo Fernandez, who previously worked under Maresca at Stamford Bridge, is expected before the end of next week’s transfer window.

And Maresca is keen to add more experience to his squad in the coming days.

“We have experienced players for sure. We have leaders,” added the Italian.

“Now we need to wait four or five more days to see if we can add one or two more captains to Ruben [Dias] and Erling [Haaland] who are the captains.”

Maresca has got off to an unconvincing start to the daunting task of succeeding Guardiola.

After a 0-3 defeat to Arsenal in the Community Shield, City needed two late goals from defenders Marc Guehi and Josko Gvardiol to edge past Bournemouth 2-1 on the opening weekend of the Premier League season.

Jeremy Doku will miss the trip to Selhurst Park due to injury, but Elliot Anderson is fit after only suffering a cramp when his league debut for the club was cut short last weekend.

August 28, 2026




 SMA moves to protect critical communication systems 







THE Spectrum Management Authority (SMA) says safeguards are being put in place to prevent Jamaica’s roll-out of fifth-generation (5G) technology from interfering with critical communication systems, including those used in aviation.

The assurance comes amid concerns about the potential for 5G services to interfere with systems operating in neighbouring frequency bands, as Jamaica prepares for wider adoption of the technology.

Managing director of the SMA Dr Maria Myers-Hamilton said the authority’s responsibility extends beyond making spectrum available for new technologies to ensuring that Jamaica’s communications environment remains safe and properly managed.

“We have to ensure that as Jamaica advances technologically, we are protecting the integrity of the spectrum and the critical services that depend on it. Ultimately, we manage the risk,” said Myers-Hamilton.

As Jamaica’s regulatory body responsible for managing the radio frequency spectrum, the SMA oversees the allocation and assignment of frequencies and monitors their use to identify and address harmful interference.

“Whenever you introduce a new technology, you have to consider what is already operating within that environment and what is operating in adjacent bands. Our job is to understand those interactions, identify where there may be a risk of interference, and put the appropriate safeguards in place,” Myers-Hamilton explained.

She pointed out that the SMA’s oversight continues after frequencies have been assigned, with its spectrum monitoring systems and technical teams used to detect, identify, and locate radio frequency signals and investigate potential sources of interference.

“We continuously monitor the spectrum because the environment is always changing. New devices are introduced, new services come on stream, and patterns of use change, so monitoring allows us to identify issues and respond where necessary,” she said.

Myers-Hamilton noted that while much of this technical work takes place behind the scenes, effective spectrum management supports communication systems Jamaicans rely on every day.

“People may not necessarily see spectrum management happening, but they experience the results of it every day. Whether you’re using your mobile phone, listening to the radio, or relying on critical communication services, spectrum is involved,” she said.

As Jamaica embraces faster and more sophisticated wireless technologies, Dr Myers-Hamilton said innovation must be balanced with the protection of existing services.

“We want Jamaica to benefit from the opportunities that technologies such as 5G can provide, but innovation has to be introduced responsibly. Our role is to create an environment where new technologies can thrive while ensuring that existing services remain protected,”added Myers-Hamilton.

 Gayle, Pinnock among Jamaicans eyeing Diamond League final 







Long jumpers Tajay Gayle and Wayne Pinnock and shot-putter Rajindra Campbell have eyes on spots at next week’s Wanda Diamond League final in Brussels, Belgium, after taking podium positions during the Weltklasse Zürich at Letzigrund Stadium in Switzerland.

Women’s 400m hurdles runner Rushell Clayton was among the Jamaican podium finishers at the meet that was the 14th and last stop in the series which began in May.

World record runs by Brazil’s Alison dos Santos, who clocked 45.80 seconds in the men’s 400m hurdles, and American Masai Russell, who timed 12.09 (0.0m/s) in the 100m hurdles, were the undoubted highlights of the day for the 25,000 people in attendance.

Gayle, who was ranked fifth in the Diamond League going into the meet, took second in a competitive men’s long jump with a best of 8.43m (-0.3m/s). He was just behind Greece’s Olympic Games and World Championships gold medalist who won with 8.45m (0.4m/s). Fourth-ranked Pinnock was third with 8.33m (0.4m/s).

Masai Russell (left) crosses the finish line to win and breaks the world record in the women’s 100m during the Diamond League athletics meeting at Letzigrund Stadium on Thursday. Also pictured is Ditaji Kambundji of Switzerland.

Campbell, who was ranked second, was runner-up in the men’s shot put with 22.22m. He had three throws over the 22-metre mark, while improving on his sixth-place finish in Silesia, Poland, on Sunday. American Jordan Geist threw a personal best 22.53m to win the event in Zurich. World leader Leonardo Fabbri of Italy finishing third with 22.16m, ending a run of six straight wins, including the final at the European Championships.

Clayton was third in the women’s 400m hurdles in 53.17, just edged on the line for second by the veteran Dalilah Muhammad of the United States who ran a season’s best 53.16. Another American Anna Cockrell took full advantage of a mishap by Slovakia’s Emma Zapletalova, winning with a world leading 52.13. Cockrell also broke the meet record 52.18 set by Femke Bol of the Netherlands last year.

Two-time World Athletics Championships gold medallist Danielle Williams ran 12.56 (0.0m/s) for fourth in the 100m hurdles, just ahead of compatriot Ackera Nugent (12.69). They were well-placed to witness the masterclass by Russell, who bettered the previous world record of 12.12 set by Nigeria’s Tobi Amusan at the 2022 World Championships. Amusan was second to Russell in a season’s best 12.23, with Nadine Visser of the Netherlands third in a season’s best 12.34.

Tina Clayton may have done enough to book her ticket to the Diamond League final after her fourth-place finish in the women’s 100m with 10.98 (-0.7m/s). Brianna Lyston was sixth with 11.13, while Jonielle Smith was seventh with 11.14. St Lucia’s Olympic Games champion Julien Alfred ran a national record 10.70 to win, lowering the 10.75 she set last year. American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, who was also timed in a season’s best 10.70 for second, was losing a 100m race for the first time since May 2024. Jefferson-Wooden’s compatriot Sha’Carrie Richardson was third with 10.97.

Brazil’s Alison dos Santos celebrates winning and breaking the world record in the men’s 400m hurdles during the Diamond League athletics meeting at Letzigrund Stadium on Thursday.

Lamara Distin was fourth in the women’s high jump with a season’s best equalling 1.96m, as Australia’s Nicola Olyslagers won with a season’s best 2.02m. Iryna Gerashchenko of Ukraine equalled her personal best 2.00m for second, while Marija Vukovic set a Montenegro national record 1.98m for third.

World Championships medallist Bryan Levell, who was racing for the first time in over a month, was sixth in the men’s 200m with 20.32 (-0.4m/s). Kenneth Bednarek of the United States set a world leading 19.62 to take the win, ahead of South Africa’s Sinesipho Dambile (19.82), while Canada’s Andre de Grasse was third with 20.03.

Commonwealth Games champion Navasky Anderson, who was making his Diamond League debut, was seventh in the men’s 800m with 1:44.31. Kenya’s Emmanuel Wanyonyi won with a world leading 1:41.76, followed by Algerians Djamel Sedjati (1:41.83) and Slimane Moula (1:43.52).

BY PAUL A REID Observer writer reidp@jamaicaobserver.com 
 August 28, 2026




 Brown’s Town High target daCosta Cup 2nd round 







Brown’s Town High’s initial goal in the upcoming ISSA daCosta Cup schoolboy football competition is to advance from the preliminary round for the first time in two seasons, according to coach Tyrone Codner.

Brown’s Town, who usually play in the competitive St Ann group, missed out on advancing last season when they needed a win in their final group game. But they lost 0-1 to Ferncourt High, who finished second behind group winners Ocho Rios High.

If Brown’s Town advance from the first round this season, they will earn a place in the first round of the Ben Francis Cup and the second round of the daCosta Cup.

Codner told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday that the team’s preseason preparation has been mostly satisfactory.

“It’s a work in progress; I would say fairly decent. We are seeing some of what we are looking for,” he said, adding that they have had some quality practice matches which he believes will make them better when the competition begins.

“The better the opposition, the harder they will work and then it will only give the boys belief going into the season,” he noted.

Brown’s Town, who are not among the seeded teams, will begin their campaign on the opening match day. Codner welcomed that, saying he prefers that his side will get competitive games before facing the top teams.

“I would say that it is a good thing starting to play early. Starting late is not always good, because teams could gather momentum, and then you are starting the season when teams are already up and running,” he explained.

“On the other hand the teams that are coming in late, they’ll have a longer preseason, which could also lead to injuries and so on. So, I don’t really have a problem with starting to play early and get a good start,” he added.

This season Brown’s Town will compete in Group C, alongside Discovery Bay High, Ferncourt High, Marcus Garvey Technical, Walkerswood Academy, York Castle High and Cedric Titus High.

The Brown’s Town head coach said his team has taken lessons from last season’s disappointment.

“We fell short on the last match of the group. We needed to win to advance, and we ended up losing one-nil. But we had some serious injuries last year that hampered our season… we were in a very tough zone.”

He believes Brown’s Town have more experience and are better prepared this season. But he expects another tightly-contested first round.

“If we do what we should do, then we should be all right. I mean, it is still going to be competitive based on what I would have seen in the Under-16 competition, because the Under-16 group was very close. We had three teams coming out, and it was very close going right into the last day, so I expect it to be close again,” he reasoned.

news.title: Trump's Iran war conduct sets dangerous international law precedent, says article
news.text: An article published by The Conversation on August 28 said the Trump administration has repeatedly acted as if it is above international law, including by claiming such law does not apply to the United States and by imposing sanctions on officials of the International Criminal Court (ICC). The article said this approach was setting a dangerous precedent.It said the US and Israel began a war against Iran six months ago in what legal scholars described as a clear violation of international law, citing Article 2 of the UN Charter, which prohibits the use or threat of force. It added that the conduct of the war since then had also come under scrutiny and said actions in Iran must be monitored, investigated and prosecuted if the evidence warrants it.The article said the body of law governing armed conflict is known as international humanitarian law, or the laws of war, and is meant to limit the means and methods of warfare to prevent suffering among combatants and civilians. It said many, though not all, violations amount to war crimes. It also said the law draws a clear distinction between civilians and combatants, and between civilian and military objects, and prohibits attacks on civilians and civilian objects such as schools, hospitals, bridges, power plants, agricultural infrastructure, dams and water treatment plants.According to the article, militaries must take "all feasible precautions" to minimise civilian deaths, injuries and damage to civilian objects, including verifying that targets are military objectives. It said a "dual-use" object can be treated as a military target only if it makes "an effective contribution to military action" and attacking it offers a "definite military advantage". Even then, it said, an attack is prohibited if it would cause disproportionate damage to civilians. The article gave the example of a bridge, saying that although it could have a military use, damage to it could severely affect civilians and a strike on it would likely amount to a war crime. It added that if there is any doubt, a site should be presumed to be a protected civilian object.The article said US President Donald Trump had repeatedly threatened to destroy bridges, power plants, oil wells and desalination plants, and had also threatened to destroy Iran's entire civilisation. It said Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth had argued for fighting wars without legal constraints, referring to what he called "stupid rules of engagement". The article also cited Hegseth as saying there would be "no quarter, no mercy for our enemies", and said ordering denial of quarter is expressly prohibited under the laws of war and amounts to a war crime.Turning to specific incidents, the article said a girls' primary school in the southern town of Minab was bombed on the opening day of the war. It said the strike took place on a Saturday morning, a school day for Iranian children, and at least 156 people were killed, including 120 children. The article said a school is unquestionably a civilian object and, with teachers and students present, the attack was also on civilians, making it unlawful on its face.It said evidence collected after the strike suggested a guided Tomahawk missile was used and noted that the US has such missiles in its arsenal while Iran does not. The article said the school was next to buildings of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which were also hit, and this could suggest mistaken targeting. It added that the Trump administration had not accepted responsibility, though an initial US assessment found US forces were "likely" behind the bombing and cited outdated targeting information. The article said the US had apparently still not carried out a comprehensive intelligence assessment or released its full investigation. It added that while Washington could argue the school was hit by mistake while targeting IRGC buildings, it appeared likely that legally required precautions and target verification had not been taken.The article also referred to strikes on water facilities. It said two water storage reservoirs near the Strait of Hormuz were damaged in June and that they supplied water to 20,000 civilians. It said it was unclear whether the US had intentionally struck the reservoirs, but added that independent experts described the weapon as a precision-guided bomb and said the remoteness of the facilities pointed to a precision strike. The article said desalination plants had also been targeted by both the US and Iran during the war. It described desalination plants and water storage facilities as essential to supplying fresh water to civilians and said attacks on them were especially serious in an arid region that often faces water shortages. Such attacks, it said, would amount to war crimes because they severely affect access to water.On accountability, the article said the ICC has no jurisdiction over the war because neither the US nor Iran is a party to the court. It said that leaves open the possibility of another country investigating and prosecuting individuals in its own domestic courts, but added that such cases are complex and politically unlikely because they could require Americans to be tried abroad. The article concluded that full investigations and prosecutions over military actions in the war should take place in both the US and Iran, saying the issue goes to the heart of accountability for possible war crimes and the wider effort to deter future violations.With PTI Inputs- EndsPublished By: India Today Web Desk Published On: Aug 28, 2026 14:46 IST

news.title: Dolly Parton brought divided Americans together. What can we learn from her? | Margaret Sullivan
news.text:
The moment that the world found out that Dolly Parton had died, I was in a hair salon in the reddest congressional district in New York state. The neighborhood on the shore of Lake Erie where I move every summer voted solidly for Donald Trump in 2024.

I often pass a lawn sign that has something misogynistic to say about New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, and the mere mention of Kamala Harris’s name can bring derisive jokes. Of course, there certainly are liberals and independents to be found, but on balance the area leans right.

On my errands around town, I’ve heard scornful comments about transgender people, and the local Catholic church where I sometimes attend mass has a priest who, during a homily this summer, praised Trump for his war in Iran.

A lot of the people I’ve chatted with around town are outspoken about being anti-vaccine.

But when cellphones started pinging with the news about Dolly, it’s not overstating things to say that everybody was devastated. Stylists and customers alike seemed to feel a personal connection – to her music, to her philanthropy, to her sheer goodness.

How did Dolly, a rags-to-riches country music superstar with a Tennessee twang and bedazzled everything, manage to endear herself to Americans of every political stripe?

What was her secret – and does it hold some wisdom for the those who seek unity in this divided nation, who appreciate civility, who believe there’s an American ethos that transcends our ugly politics?

Some of it, surely, was that she had a gift for poking fun at herself, and joining in the laughter, as when she would say she didn’t mind being called a dumb blonde because she knew, after all, that she wasn’t dumb – and that she wasn’t a blonde. After her illness made headlines last year, she took to social media to make a simple point: “I ain’t dead yet.” She called herself a “Backwoods Barbie” in a song of that name.

Then there was her remarkable generosity. Her organization, Imagination Library, gave more than 330m books to children around the world. She founded it, in part, she said, because her father couldn’t read or write.

She never forgot where she came from, as she raised money for a new hospital in her home country in Tennessee, or offered $500 awards to local teenagers when they graduated from high school.

Still, how did she manage not to alienate the Maga world when she promoted the Covid-19 vaccine (the research for which she had helped fund)?

Again, the humor helped, as when she changed the words of one of her most famous songs, Jolene to something that rhymed, and sang “vaccine, vaccine” in promotional videos. You had to smile, and maybe decide to get the jab, or at least to tolerate those who did. And she never made it political.

“She practiced a unique brand of radical acceptance,” wrote Jad Abumrad in a New York Times essay this week. “No one would ever be thrown out of the Big Dolly Tent.”

And, though she is being mourned as something of an angel on earth, she was a razor-sharp businessperson. She was smart and savvy about it all, as befitted the superstar who chalked up 25 No 1 country singles over the years.

As Abumrad learned while interviewing and observing her at length as he created the podcast Dolly Parton’s America, she always told her own story.

“If a male talkshow host made a joke about her figure, she’d make an ever better joke about it. She was always two steps ahead of you. She never allowed herself to be a part of a story of which she was not the author.”

Can what Dolly Parton did be bottled somehow? Can her serendipitous mixture of humor, humility and humanity be sprinkled over our troubled waters to calm and soothe them?

Probably not – there is only one Dolly Parton – but that doesn’t mean we can’t learn something from this rare individual.

The rest of us might channel Dolly a bit more, and remember that a self-deprecating joke goes a long way toward easing tensions. We might recognize that financial success need not turn into ego glorification or arrogance.

And most of all, we might keep in mind that genuine generosity – if it comes from the heart – has the power to transcend politics.

Dolly Parton’s legacy, of course, resides in her wonderful songs, from Coat of Many Colors to 9 to 5. That’s what she would want.

But I don’t think she’d object if we also kept in mind her authentic kindness, her disarming wit – and the “radical acceptance” that fueled it all.

 Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

I often pass a lawn sign that has something misogynistic to say about New York’s Democratic governor, Kathy Hochul, and the mere mention of Kamala Harris’s name can bring derisive jokes. Of course, there certainly are liberals and independents to be found, but on balance the area leans right.
