news.title: Trump Offers Aid to Nepal as 90 Americans Remain Unaccounted For After Deadly Floods
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has offered Nepal “any help that they need” after a devastating flash flood and debris surge struck the Nepal-Tibet border region on August 26, killing at least 469 people in Nepal and leaving nearly 1,000 unaccounted for across Nepal and Tibet. 

Trump described the destruction as “brutal”, saying even “strong, well-built buildings” were swept away. He initially said 50–60 Americans were in the affected area, while the US State Department later said it was tracking around 90 Americans who may have been impacted and remained unaccounted for; three Americans had been rescued and no US citizen death had been confirmed at the time. 

Washington has offered humanitarian assistance, including $500,000 in emergency funding and a disaster-response adviser. Meanwhile, Nepali and Chinese authorities continue search operations amid severe infrastructure damage and the threat of further flooding after a barrier lake began overflowing.

‘Brutal’ Destruction Across Nepal

Trump’s offer came as rescue workers faced one of the most challenging disasters to hit Nepal in recent years. Speaking to reporters on August 27, Trump said the US had contacted Nepal’s leadership and made clear that Washington was ready to provide whatever assistance was required.

“We’ve called Nepal, and we’ve offered any help that they need,” Trump said, adding that the US has a “very good relationship” with Nepal. Describing the disaster as “brutal”, he said the scale of destruction was difficult to comprehend, particularly after seeing strong structures destroyed by the force of the floodwaters.

“There were 50, maybe 60 Americans over there,” Trump said, referring to US citizens believed to have been in the affected region. He added that authorities had not yet received a complete list of those affected and expressed hope that the Americans were safe.

The figure subsequently rose in US government assessments. A State Department spokesperson said officials were tracking approximately 90 Americans who may have been impacted and were currently unaccounted for. Three Americans had been rescued, while the department said it was not aware of any US citizen de@ths.

A Disaster Still Unfolding

The disaster began on August 26 in the mountainous border region between Nepal and Tibet, when a massive surge of water, ice, rock and mud swept downstream through river valleys. Nepal’s Rasuwa district was among the worst-hit areas, with the flood destroying homes, bridges, roads and power infrastructure.

The US Geological Survey has attributed the event to a glacial collapse that generated an enormous debris flow, rather than an earthquake. Earlier reports had suggested seismic activity, but subsequent analysis indicated that the movement of ice and rock itself produced the seismic signals detected during the disaster.

By August 28, the confirmed de@th toll in Nepal had risen to 469, with nearly 1,000 people still missing across Nepal and neighbouring Tibet. At least 540 foreigners were among those unaccounted for, according to Reuters. The figures remain fluid as rescue teams reach isolated locations and authorities reconcile separate lists of missing people.

Many of those missing were tourists and pilgrims travelling through the Himalayan region, including people heading towards Mount Kailash in Tibet. The presence of large numbers of international travellers has prompted governments across the world to launch efforts to locate their citizens.

For American families, the uncertainty has been particularly distressing. The Associated Press reported that around 90 Americans were unaccounted for, including people travelling as part of pilgrimage groups. The Isha Foundation also said 22 Americans associated with its group were missing after communications were lost in the affected region. Families and friends have turned to social media in the hope of receiving information about relatives whose whereabouts remain unknown.

US Aid As Rescue Efforts Continue

The US response began even before Trump’s public offer of further assistance. On August 26, the State Department expressed condolences to families affected by the disaster and announced that it was deploying a disaster-response adviser to support relief operations.

Washington also committed $500,000 in emergency assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services. The funding is intended to provide emergency shelter, relief supplies and water, sanitation and hygiene assistance to communities affected by the flooding.

The US Embassy in Kathmandu is working with Nepali authorities and other contacts to account for American citizens in the affected region. The State Department has also urged Americans in Nepal to follow instructions from local authorities and monitor official information as rescue operations continue.

The immediate challenge, however, is not limited to locating missing people. The destruction of roads and bridges has made several areas difficult to access, while damage to power infrastructure and communications has complicated coordination.

Thousands of Nepali security personnel have been involved in search-and-rescue efforts, with helicopters and heavy machinery being used where conditions permit. But the terrain remains dangerous, with unstable slopes, debris and blocked river channels creating further risks for both survivors and rescuers.

The situation became even more precarious on August 28 when a barrier lake formed by debris began overflowing. Reuters reported that the lake’s water volume had risen above 2.5 million cubic metres, prompting evacuations and forcing some rescue operations to pause because of fears of another downstream surge.

Nepal has received offers of international assistance, but authorities have indicated that the country will continue to lead rescue operations internally for now. International governments and humanitarian organisations are nevertheless providing financial, medical and logistical support.

The Logical Indian’s Perspective

Natural disasters do not recognise borders, nationalities or political differences. In Nepal, the same floodwaters that destroyed homes and infrastructure also left foreign tourists, pilgrims and local residents facing the same fear and uncertainty. The immediate priority must therefore remain saving lives, locating missing people and ensuring that relief reaches communities without discrimination.

Trump’s offer of assistance, alongside the US government’s emergency funding and efforts to locate American citizens, underlines the importance of international solidarity when a disaster overwhelms local capacity. At the same time, Nepal’s leadership of its own rescue operations should be respected, with outside support provided in ways that strengthen not complicate local relief efforts.

news.title: Judge blocks rule implementing Trump plan to restrict mail-in voting
news.text:
A federal judge on Thursday blocked the ​US Postal Service from implementing core parts of a new rule it adopted at President Donald Trump’s direction that would ‌tighten mail-in voting requirements ahead of the November congressional elections.

US District Judge Indira Talwani in Boston issued a temporary restraining order, opens new tab at the behest of Democratic-led states and voting rights groups after the US Supreme Court on Monday issued a ruling that led to the lifting of earlier injunctions blocking Trump’s plans to restrict mail-in voting.

That decision led to ​a frantic effort by dozens of Democratic state attorneys general and voting rights groups including the League of Women Voters to renew ​their legal fight and secure an order that would prevent the USPS from enforcing a rule that was allowed ⁠to take effect on Wednesday.

In Thursday’s ruling, Talwani said the rule risked preventing citizens from casting ballots by mail unless states secure the Postal ​Service’s sign-off on the envelopes used for that purpose and upload information on each voter into an electronic portal run by the agency.

The judge said ​the agency had presented no evidence regarding fraudulent mail-in voting that would necessitate such a rule, which she said likely was unlawful and adopted in violation of the US Constitution, which gives states the authority to administer elections.

“USPS’s interest in correcting an unsubstantiated problem through likely unconstitutional means is dwarfed by the overwhelming risk of pervasive ​disenfranchisement of citizens who need access to mail ballots in order to vote,” she wrote.

The restraining order Talwani issued will remain in place for 14 ​days while she considers whether to issue a longer-term preliminary injunction blocking the rule. 

The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Barack Obama, plans to consider whether to ‌do so ⁠during a September 3 hearing.

“Today’s order presses pause on an unlawful power grab that would sow chaos and confusion for the millions of voters who depend on mail ballots,” Sophia Lin Lakin, a lawyer for the voting rights groups at the American Civil Liberties Union, said in a statement.

The White House and USPS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

USPS issued the rule to implement an executive order the Republican president signed in March ​after years of Trump calling for ​tighter rules on voting by ⁠mail and pushing the false claim that his 2020 presidential election defeat to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of widespread voter fraud.

Under the rule, states must supply the USPS with lists of mail ballot recipients, and ​all outbound and return ballot envelopes must bear unique barcodes. 

The USPS, under the rule, may refuse to ​deliver ballots that ⁠do not comply with the new standards or are associated with voters who do not appear on the lists.

All 50 states allow for some form of mail-in voting, with 29 allowing voters to ask to cast ballots that way without providing a reason and eight conducting their elections entirely by mail.

During the ⁠2024 election, ​the USPS says it processed nearly 100 million ballots, and about 30% of voters nationwide ​cast ballots by mail, according to the states.

They argue the new federal restrictions risk disenfranchising voters and would unduly burden states in the weeks running up to the election, forcing ​them to buy new envelopes and equipment, establish new systems and train staff.
news.summary: US District Judge Indira Talwani blocked a USPS rule backed by Donald Trump that would have restricted mail-in voting ahead of the election.
news.author: Reuters

news.title: Trump Navy Punishes Teen Sailor After Suicide Attempt at Sea
news.text:
A 19-year-old sailor who leapt from the USS Abraham Lincoln in what has been described as an apparent suicide attempt earlier this month is now facing disciplinary action from Donald Trump’s Navy after spending months stuck at sea during the Iran war.

The servicemember, who is married and has two young children, is being subjected to non-judicial punishment for alleged violations of the military code, his wife said, according to charging documents reviewed by MS NOW.

According to the account, the sailor went overboard during a mental health crisis, apparently trying to drown himself as conditions aboard the aircraft carrier continued to worsen.

Crew members on the Lincoln have reportedly been living with mold in showers, malfunctioning toilets, laundry service failures, limited food supplies and extended periods without hot water.

Navy charging documents accuse the sailor of “intentionally faking an illness or hurting themselves to avoid work, duty or service.” A separate allegation says he did not report to his assigned place of duty during the mental health episode.

“I think they’re insane for doing this to people who need mental help,” the sailor’s wife told MS NOW. “Instead of giving them help, this is just another huge stressor.”

She said her husband had repeatedly asked for paternity leave so he could meet his newborn daughter for the first time, but every request was denied. His case is now set to be handled at a “captain’s mast,” where his commanding officer could withhold up to half of his pay, according to the documents.

The sailor was pulled from the water after going overboard on August 3 and was medically evacuated, his wife said. He returned to San Diego 10 days later.

He then spent five days at Naval Medical Center San Diego, known locally as Balboa, where staff monitored his vital signs but never had him evaluated by a psychiatrist or therapist, she said.

He was ordered back to work immediately after his release and did not receive his first therapy session until this Wednesday, nearly two weeks after arriving home.

The Navy is pursuing the case through non-judicial punishment, an internal disciplinary process generally used for lower-level misconduct that avoids a formal court-martial and criminal conviction.

The Daily Mail has contacted the Pentagon for comment. 

The Lincoln has spent more than 250 consecutive days at sea, with conditions worsening after the Iran war diverted the carrier to the Middle East. 

An Iranian attack destroyed a crucial supply hub in Bahrain, forcing provisions to travel 2,200 miles from Diego Garcia.

Amid mounting public outcry, the Navy is sending additional counselors and social workers to the Lincoln, while giving its exhausted crew a rest-and-recovery stop in Thailand next week before the carrier returns home.

The Navy also dispatched the USS George Washington from Japan to take over the Lincoln’s mission in the Middle East. 

Both Trump and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have repeatedly denied reports of severe conditions aboard the Lincoln. 

While taking questions from reporters earlier this month, the president dismissed concerns from sailors’ families before declaring the Lincoln’s record deployment was ‘not nearly long enough.’

Hegseth called reports of poor conditions ‘completely misrepresented’ and insisted the Navy gives every crew ‘everything we can provide them at every single moment.’

A bipartisan group of Congressional lawmakers, meanwhile, has demanded greater oversight and transparency over living conditions aboard the carrier.

Canada PM says it will be Lake Ontario ‘then, now and always’ after Trump's ‘Lake America’ order

Mark Carney noted that the name is over 400 years old and predates the formation of both the US and Canada.

9.20am, 28 Aug 2026

Share options

CANADA PRIME MINISTER Mark Carney has said that his country “know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario”, after Donald Trump ordered it to be renamed “Lake America”.

The name change order from the US president came as he escalated his trade war with Canada.

US-Canada trade talks collapsed at the last-minute last week, which prompted the two longtime allies to slap tit-for-tat tariffs on each other.

On Thursday, Trump signed an executive order changing the name of the body of water on the border between the North American neighbours.

“We’re going to be changing the name of Lake Ontario effective immediately to Lake America,” Trump told journalists as he signed the order at the White House.

Asked by a reporter why he was targeting an ally for punishment instead of America’s adversaries, Trump replied: “The Canadian officials have treated us very badly. They’re nasty people.”

Behind Trump’s desk in the Oval Office were two maps – one with the words “Lake America” in red over the lake, and the other with the header, “Making the Great Lakes Even Greater.”

Poster shows name change from Lake Ontario to Lake America, as Trump signs executive order on renaming in Oval Office of the White HouseAlamy Stock Photo

Alamy Stock Photo

In a post on social media, Carney remarked that the name Lake Ontario “comes from the Wendat word Ontari’io”.

He said this “appropriately means “the lake is beautiful, the lake is big”.

Meanwhile, Carney noted that the name is over 400 years old and predates the formation of both the United States and Canada.

“We know that America is changing,” said Carney. “Their trading relationships, their foreign policies, their national monuments, their hydronyms.

Advertisement

“Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always.”

Lake Ontario is the smallest by surface area of the five Great Lakes, which straddle the border between the United States and Canada. It borders the Canadian province of Ontario and the US state of New York.

The name change mirrors Trump’s unilateral altering of the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America in January 2025 – a move Mexico has also rejected.

In Toronto, Canada’s largest city which lies on the lake’s northwestern shore, Canadians and Americans alike criticised Trump’s move.

“Typical Trump. He’s being a bully, he goads, he antagonizes,” said Mark Weicker, who lives in Kitchener, west of Toronto.

“He’s just trying to egg us on,” chimed in Jake Marchuk, who was visiting from Alberta province.

Megan Smith, who hails from New Jersey, put it bluntly: “It just makes him look stupid.”

Trump’s executive order meanwhile tells the US Department of the Interior to update references to the lake in the official geographical naming service within 30 days and ensure the federal government calls it “Lake America”.

It justified the name change by saying that the deepest part of the lake is on the American side, meaning that the US “claims most of the Lake’s volume.”

BREAKING: President Trump officially changes the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

"If you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean." 👀 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/OZOmfibisP— The White House (@WhiteHouse) August 27, 2026 

Trump has even hinted at renaming oceans that border the US.

“We have a gulf and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.

“So, maybe we’ll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we’ll change them both.”

news.title: US Couple Missing in Nepal Flood as Daughters Seek Answers
news.text:
The daughters of a Texas couple missing in the Himalayas are anxiously searching for answers after their parents disappeared during a once-in-a-lifetime pilgrimage, as catastrophic flooding swept through the Nepal-Tibet border region and killed at least 472 people.

Deepak and Madhu Ahuja are among 90 Americans still unaccounted for following Wednesday’s disaster, which has left more than 1,500 people missing across Nepal and Tibet while rescue teams comb through the battered mountain terrain.

Their daughters, Ashna and Shreya Ahuja, said the couple had stayed in steady contact throughout their journey to sacred Mount Kailash before communication abruptly stopped.

‘We hope that they have been found and are at a hospital and are safe,’ Ashna told CNN, as the family pressed US officials and contacts in the region for updates.

The sisters are gathered with relatives at their aunt’s home, waiting for any sign that their parents made it through the devastation alive.

‘The latest honestly hasn’t changed too much in the past two days,’ Ashna said.

‘We are still reaching out to both officials at the Beijing embassy, Kathmandu embassy, and speaking to people on the ground there to see what the efforts are looking like to rescue and save our parents, hopefully.’

So far, however, Ashna said the family has received little in the way of ‘concrete information.’

Shreya last spoke to her parents only hours before they headed toward the border crossing on August 26.

At the time, there was no indication of the catastrophe about to unfold.

‘They had just finished the pilgrimage,’ she recalled. ‘They were feeling really proud of themselves for having completed it.’

Deepak and Madhu had also just met the religious spiritual leader who led the trek and felt ‘very blessed’ by the encounter.

Most of all, they were looking forward to getting back to their family.

‘They were ready to come home,’ Shreya said.

The couple told their daughter that their tour group was heading toward the border. Because it was nighttime back in the US, Shreya went to bed believing her parents were continuing their journey as planned.

‘I thought nothing of it,’ she said.

Hours later, the region was being consumed by a disaster of almost unimaginable proportions.

‘We just love them a lot and want them to come home,’ the sisters told the BBC, through tears.

By Friday morning, authorities said at least 472 people had died across Nepal and Tibet, while more than 1,500 remained missing.

More than 3,250 people have been rescued by helicopter, while over 150 injured survivors have been taken to hospitals in Kathmandu and the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading.

In Tibet, Chinese state media reported three deaths and 558 people missing in Gyirong County, including 260 foreign nationals.

The US State Department said 90 Americans remained unaccounted for across Nepal and China. 

No American deaths had been confirmed as of the latest update, while three US citizens had been rescued.

The Ahujas daughters along with many other families are clinging onto a sliver of hope. 

Connectivity across the devastated region has been severely disrupted, meaning some of those currently listed as missing could ultimately be found alive and well.

For Ashna and Shreya, every hour without news is nevertheless excruciating.

‘It’s definitely a terrifying situation,’ Ashna said. ‘We know that the people on the ground are doing their best efforts, and we hope that they stay safe as they continue to do so.’

The trip had particular significance for the family because Deepak had dreamed of completing the demanding Mount Kailash pilgrimage before getting older.

It was a bucket-list journey timed around his 60th birthday.

‘He wanted to do this trip before or, you know, right when he turned 60,’ Ashna explained. 

‘He didn’t know how his body would change as he grew older. And it’s a pretty tough trek.’

Madhu was initially nervous about whether she could complete the journey herself, her daughter said, but was determined to accompany her husband.

‘She really, really wanted to support him and make sure that he got the best 60th birthday possible,’ Ashna said.

A video filmed by Madhu captured Deepak meditating at Lake Manasarovar near Mount Kailash during what should have been the culmination of their extraordinary journey.

‘She could see how happy he was just being there at the lake,’ their daughter said.

The Ahujas are far from the only American family clinging to hope as they wait for news from Nepal.

New Yorkers Ramesh Sharma, 65, and his wife Neelam, 64, are also missing after traveling to the region for their own Mount Kailash pilgrimage.

Their daughter, Dr. Radhika Sharma, said the journey was her parents’ first vacation alone since retiring last year.

‘My parents have been wanting to do this for a while,’ she previously told Our News Outlet.

‘They had retired last year, and they just started traveling and really living their life.’

The family believes Ramesh and Neelam were near the border at around 8am – about one hour before the flooding – but has been unable to determine what happened next.

‘We don’t know why they were delayed,’ Radhika said. ‘We are hoping that they made it to the Tibet side.’

Speaking separately to the BBC, she described the torment of searching for information from thousands of miles away.

‘I am just trying to find them, I don’t have any answers,’ she said. ‘No one has any answers.’

Hundreds of other foreign tourists and pilgrims from countries including Canada, Britain and Australia have also been caught up in the catastrophe.

Nepalese officials have warned that the numbers could continue changing as rescue teams reach isolated communities and communications are restored.

The disaster sent enormous quantities of water, ice, rock and debris roaring through the mountainous border region, obliterating communities and destroying roads and bridges.

Authorities are also watching for the possibility of further flooding as unstable debris and landslide dams threaten areas already devastated by Wednesday’s surge.

On Thursday, President Donald Trump said that the US had offered Nepal whatever assistance it needed.

‘We are sending aid and we’ve spoken to the leadership,’ Trump said. ‘And we let them know anything they want, we’ll have.’

news.title: Ottawa considers replacing Trump Avenue with ‘Taco’ or ‘Obama’ Avenue
news.text:
Councillor Riley Brockington raised the issue during an Ottawa City Council meeting on Wednesday, arguing that a street in the national capital should no longer bear the name of U.S. President Donald Trump.

Trump Avenue is located in Ottawa’s Central Park neighbourhood, where several streets have names inspired by New York City, including Manhattan Crescent, Staten Street and Madison Park.

Residents previously considered changing the name in 2021. The vote ended in a 21-21 tie, while 20 households abstained. Under Ottawa policy, support from at least 50% plus one is required to rename a street.

Brockington said he intends to work with residents on a community-led renaming process during the next term of council.

Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe also expressed support for removing Trump’s name, provided residents back the change.

The debate comes amid worsening Canada-U.S. trade relations. Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Canada recently walked away from negotiations on a new trade agreement and announced dollar-for-dollar counter-tariffs on hundreds of American goods in response to new U.S. duties.
news.summary: Ottawa City Council is considering removing U.S. President Donald Trump’s name from a residential street in Canada’s capital, with “Taco Avenue” and “Obama Avenue” among the suggested replacements, as tensions between Canada and the United States continue to escalate, a Qazinform News Agency correspondent.

news.title: U.S., S. Korea, Japan to hold Freedom Edge drills in September
news.text:
SEOUL, Aug. 28 (UPI) -- The United States, South Korea and Japan will kick off their annual Freedom Edge trilateral military exercise on Sept. 7, Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said Friday.

The multi-domain drills will run through Sept. 11 and will be held in international waters east and south of South Korea's Jeju Island, the JCS said in a message to reporters.

"This exercise is a defensive exercise conducted annually by the three nations to counter North Korea's nuclear and missile threats and to safeguard regional peace and stability," the message said.

The announcement comes after Seoul and Washington cut short their joint Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise following an order by U.S. President Donald Trump aimed at restarting direct diplomacy with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

Trump last week abruptly ordered the allies to curtail the exercise, citing its cost and saying the drills sent an "inappropriate and hostile" signal to Pyongyang. The exercise was subsequently shortened by almost a week.

North Korea routinely denounces joint military drills as rehearsals for an invasion and has carried out weapons tests around major allied exercises. Pyongyang last year called Freedom Edge "the most comprehensive and offensive war drill for aggression in its scale, content and nature."

U.S. Forces Japan said this year's iteration of Freedom Edge represented the allies' "most advanced trilateral cooperation to date."

"Freedom Edge 26 will significantly expand trilateral interoperability across multiple domains," USFJ said in a statement. "Crucially, this year's iteration features enhanced real-time data sharing and synchronized coordination among all three nations to defend against evolving regional threats."

The exercise will also include multinational maritime and aviation capabilities, enhanced air defense scenarios, medical evacuation training and maritime interdiction operations, USFJ said.

North Korea has so far shown little inclination to engage with Trump's overtures. Kim Yo Jong, the sister of Kim Jong Un, said last week that Pyongyang had "no interest" in the reduction of the U.S.-South Korea drills.

On Thursday, North Korea condemned U.S. approval of a possible $125 million sale of Sidewinder missiles and related equipment to South Korea, warning of a "serious, immediate and powerful response."

Freedom Edge emerged from a trilateral summit at Camp David in August 2023, where the then-leaders of the three countries agreed to expand security cooperation. The first Freedom Edge exercise was held in June 2024.
news.summary: The United States, South Korea and Japan will kick off their annual Freedom Edge trilateral military exercise on Sept. 7, Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said Friday.

news.title: Ad blames Acton for isolating dying mom during COVID. There's more to it
news.text:
A new ad from Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign features a GOP activist who blames Amy Acton for isolating her late mother during the COVID-19 pandemic, but records show the woman lived in Kentucky and died weeks after Ohio ended its stay-at-home order.

Ramaswamy and Acton, who served as Ohio Department of Health director in 2020 during the pandemic, are locked in a contentious race to replace Gov. Mike DeWine.

In Ramaswamy's ad, Linda Caudill, a member of the Ohio Republican Party State Central Committee, said her mother went into a nursing home shortly before Acton "shut down the state" and died two months later.

"My mother didn't understand it," Caudill said in the ad. "It traumatized her. She didn't know why her family couldn't come visit her. Two months later, she died. Amy Acton is to blame for this. It happened to a lot of families, and it shouldn't have happened. I will never forgive Amy Acton for what she did to my family."

The ad doesn't identify the nursing home or specify where Caudill's mother spent her final months. But her obituary, first reported by the liberal website TiffinOhio.net and verified by the statehouse bureau, indicates she was from Erlanger, Kentucky; belonged to a church in Elsmere, Kentucky; and died July 25, 2020, at a hospice facility in Edgewood, Kentucky, six weeks after Acton stepped down as health director.

Additional public records list northern Kentucky addresses for Caudill's mother that date back decades.

The woman's death also came two months after DeWine lifted Ohio's stay-at-home order and travel restrictions, though officials encouraged high-risk people to stay home when possible. The order, when it was in effect, included exceptions for Ohioans who needed to care for elderly loved ones.

Caudill did not respond to multiple messages seeking an interview.

“Families across Ohio were kept from dying loved ones because of Amy Acton's COVID lockdown policies," said Ramaswamy spokesperson Evan Machan. "Those families will never get that time back, and for her to now smear a devoted daughter in an effort to escape her own record is disgraceful."

COVID politics dominate Ohio governor's race

Ramaswamy has repeatedly targeted Acton's tenure as health director, blaming her for the closure of schools and businesses at the onset of the pandemic. DeWine, a Republican who appointed Acton to the job in 2019, said he bears full responsibility for his administration's decisions.

And Ohio wasn't alone.

In Kentucky, Gov. Andy Beshear stopped in-person visits to nursing homes and other long-term care facilities in March 2020, with exceptions for people receiving end-of-life care. The state allowed visits to resume in July 2020 under strict parameters, provided the facility had gone 28 days without an infection among employees or residents, the Lexington Herald-Leader reported.

At the federal level, President Donald Trump's administration directed nursing homes to halt visitors "except in certain compassionate cases."

"Vivek Ramaswamy built a career out of scamming people and lying," said Addie Bullock, a spokesperson for Acton's campaign. "His campaign has been no different."

Caudill is no stranger to Republican politics in Ohio. She served as a delegate for Trump in 2016 and 2024. She also sparked controversy as a volunteer for former U.S. Rep. Jim Renacci's 2017 campaign for governor, in part for sharing a meme that suggested violence against then-Secretary of State Jon Husted.

Caudill can be seen in a viral photo of protesters gathered outside the Ohio Statehouse on April 13, 2020, to oppose DeWine's pandemic policies.

State government reporter Jessie Balmert contributed to this report.

State government reporter Haley BeMiller can be reached at hbemiller@usatodayco.com or @haleybemiller on X.

news.title: The US needs more aluminium and it needs it now
news.text:
AgenciesThe US needs more aluminium and it needs it now

London: The U.S. "desperately" needs more aluminium, President Donald Trump told a ​virtual rally for Mike Mazzei, who has just won the Republican nomination for ​governor of Oklahoma. The state is home to a massive new smelter project, a joint venture between U.S. producer Century Aluminum and Emirates Global Aluminium (EGA).The project is ​backed by $500 million in federal funds and is exactly the sort of headline-grabbing investment Trump was hoping for when he hiked aluminium import tariffs to 50% in June last year.Also read: Reliance explores aluminium entry as Adani lines up $11.5 billion bet: ReportThe problem, though, is that even if construction at the Inola site begins on schedule by the end of this year, the plant will only begin producing hot metal in three years' time at the very earliest.That is far too long a wait for the Pentagon.Live EventsWAR GAMESThe Department of Defense (DoD) ran a wargame ‌in July last year to examine ⁠the country's ⁠aluminium resilience in the event of a large-scale conflict in 2027.Eighty participants were drawn from the aluminium supply chain, industry associations and several government departments.Favoured policy options included the obvious ones, such as building new smelters, revamping old ones and recycling more. All of which ​would improve "overall aluminum industry outcomes", the authors of the Defense Logistics Agency's (DLA) report on the exercise noted.But, they cautioned, none would meet the DoD's "shorter-term aluminium and HPA requirements within two years."HPA stands for high-purity aluminium, and it's a particular cause for concern among Pentagon planners.PRECISION HITThe U.S. defense sector accounts for only around 5% of domestic aluminium demand, but its share is "significantly higher" when it comes to HPA, which in alloy form is used in some of the Pentagon's most essential systems.There's only one domestic HPA producer, leaving the Pentagon heavily dependent on imports, most of which come from the United Arab Emirates, according to the DLA report. Or at ​least they did until Iran bombed EGA's Al Taweelah smelter in March. The smelter is being repaired, with a quarter of its electrolytic ⁠cells now operational, ‌EGA announced on Wednesday.But U.S. imports from the UAE have dropped sharply since the attack and it will take time for the smelter to return to ​full capacity.Ironically, the DoD ran a second ​wargame with only government participants, examining disruption scenarios such as outages at Alcoa's smelter in New York and Arconic's HPA plant in Iowa.The scenarios did not include ⁠a hostile attack on the largest overseas supplier of HPA to the U.S. military.The one short-term solution to come ​out of the wargame - stockpiling HPA and its alloys - just got a lot harder.COMPETITIONThe Pentagon's HPA headache is part of a broader problem. Restoring ​U.S. aluminium production capacity is a long-term task. But the market needs more metal now.The impact of tariffs on domestic production has been modest so far.Century has reactivated 50,000 tons of annual capacity at its Mount Holly smelter in South Carolina, returning the plant to full-capacity production.Magnitude 7 Metals is reopening a 1970s-era smelter in Missouri after closing it in 2024. The first 75,000-ton-per-year potline is targeted for restart by the end of the year. There has been lots of investment in recycling capacity, a section of the supply chain that saw job growth exceed 20% between 2024 and 2026, according to the Aluminum Association.But the domestic supply gap remains large. U.S. import dependence was 60% last year, according to the U.S. Geological Survey.The stress is manifest in the U.S. Midwest Premium, which is the surcharge over the London Metal Exchange price paid ‌by U.S. buyers of physical metal. The CME spot premium is $2,467 per ton, which is some $850 per ton higher than the implied 50% tariff level.The loss of production in the Gulf has triggered a scramble for metal globally, and U.S. buyers find themselves in competition with both Europe and Asia for spare units.ASK A FRIENDThe Trump administration ​has just put another aluminium smelter ​incentive on the table in the form of a ⁠reduced 25% import tariff for anyone building, expanding or refurbishing domestic smelter capacity. Canada, on the other hand, won't get a similar anticipated reduction after trade talks broke down, leading to tariff escalation rather than de-escalation.Also read: Aluminium signals recovery after correction; supply risks and energy concerns may drive the next leg higherThe country remains the largest supplier of primary aluminium to the U.S. market, although it has directed more volumes to Europe in recent months.But even if Canada could and wanted to export its entire production ​over the border, it still wouldn't be enough to fill the U.S. shortfall, according to analysts at Morgan Stanley. The marginal import ton would still be subject to a 50% tariff rate, and the Midwest premium would reflect that.However, Canada does offer one short-term solution to U.S. military planners' aluminium headache, as the DLA report points out.If the U.S. needed to surge aluminium production during a large-scale conflict, a memorandum of understanding between the two countries includes a special arrangement under which Canada would prioritize U.S. defense purchases.The Pentagon may have to ask nicely, though.The opinions expressed here are those of Andy Home, a columnist for Reuters.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Listen: Could Iceland join the EU?
news.text:
Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below:

On Saturday, Icelanders will go to the polls to answer this question: Should Iceland restart the EU accession process?

The country could match the EU criteria quite quickly, but is it willing to do so? And what would this mean for Europeans and Icelanders?

Iceland is no stranger to the EU. It is already a member of the European Economic Area, the Schengen Area, as well as the European Free Trade Association.

To put it simply, all of this means that Iceland already benefits greatly from the single market, and that one can travel easily between Iceland, and the EU.

But being an EU member has many more advantages. That’s why, back in 2009, Iceland applied for EU membership. It was well on track to complete all the requirements, but due to political changes in the years that followed, Iceland finally withdrew its application in 2015.

Now, the government coalition in power has promised to hold a referendum on EU membership. So here we are.

What do the polls say?

The latest polls suggest a very tight race, with, for now, backers of EU accession winning by a narrow margin. It’s worth saying, though, that a large number of Icelanders are still undecided.

So what if Icelanders actually decide they want to join the EU?

It’s worth remembering that this would only relaunch the negotiations. Which doesn’t guarantee the membership. But let’s assume that the accession process goes well.

Iceland would be the smallest country in the bloc, with only around 400,000 inhabitants. Malta already has more than 500,000 people.

But from an economic point of view, Iceland is richer than Malta. Its GDP is around €34bn, whereas Malta, the current smallest member, is at around €20bn.

Tourism, services, and fishing

Iceland’s economy is largely driven by tourism, services and the fishing industry.

And the country also takes advantage of its very green energy to process and transform raw materials, before exporting them.

There isn’t a particularly huge amount of raw materials in Iceland, but there is huge potential to process them using, for example, green hydropower. This is how Iceland exports a lot of aluminium.

This particular aspect is relevant for the EU, because Europeans are struggling both to mine and process raw materials.

Of course, this industry in Iceland is relatively small compared to those of other large countries. But it could still be interesting. It could contribute to the EU’s efforts to reduce its dependence on China.

Now, for Icelanders, what would EU membership mean?

Economically, this would not be a game changer, since Iceland already benefits from the single market and has a thriving economy.

Unlike some other candidates for EU membership, Iceland should be a net contributor in financial terms. What does that mean? It means that the country would send more money to the EU budget than it would receive in grants.

Aside from the economy, Iceland could be interested in getting closer to the EU for geopolitical reasons. We’ve seen how Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened Greenland, which holds a strategic position and has useful resources.

While Iceland has not been clearly threatened, it holds a similar position then Greenland, and it has reasons to be concerned.

For all these reasons, it will be interesting to see the result of the referendum this Saturday.

And in case Icelanders vote no, they will continue to be close neighbours and allies of the EU, just like Norway.

news.title: U.S. trade war is looming over sovereignty debate in Quebec election
news.text:
Charles Rousseau says he’s always believed in Quebec independence but it won’t be his top priority at the ballot box come Oct. 5, when the province chooses its next government.

In an interview outside a sovereigntist-themed coffee shop in Montreal on Thursday, the 27-year-old Masters’ student said he expects the tariff war and negotiations with American President Donald Trump to be top of mind for Quebecers during the electoral campaign. 

“What has really dominated political discourse lately is inflation, the cost of living,” he said. “I get the impression that the sovereignty movement is losing some of its momentum as well. So, people are clearly concerned about this whole conflict.”

He added that despite having two parties making sovereignty a top priority, he’s “not interested in the proposals currently on the table.”

Rousseau’s concerns appear to reflect a shift in political messaging that is already emerging after the first day of the Quebec election campaign.

For months, it seemed the provincial election could hinge on the question of a sovereignty referendum. Parti Québécois leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who has been leading in public opinion polls since 2023, promised a referendum on the issue in his first term if elected.

But the trade war with the United States is changing electoral priorities, experts say. 

A new report released by National Bank a few days before the campaign began found that Quebec is facing the highest effective tariff rate on exports among all of the provinces.

It’s a situation that already appears to be placing St-Pierre Plamondon on the defensive as his opponents argue it would be unwise to separate while Trump is threatening Canadian sovereignty.

“My opponent is named Donald Trump,” said incumbent premier Christine Fréchette after dissolving the legislature on Thursday. 

“He’s the real adversary.”

With polls showing that only about 30 per cent of Quebecers would vote for sovereignty in a referendum, St-Pierre Plamondon may need to appeal to federalist voters to win the election.

A week before the campaign began, he announced that a PQ government would not call a referendum until Trump is out of office in 2029.

Speaking to journalists Thursday, the PQ leader said his party would propose the best platform to weather the economic uncertainty caused by the trade war with the U.S. But, he urged Quebecers not to let Trump dictate the result of the election. 

“Do not allow the Trump administration’s tactics to rob us of this important debate. Do not allow our election to be hijacked,” he said. “At the end of the day, it is up to us, the people of Quebec, to decide our future and our destiny.”

Ruba Ghazal, parliamentary leader of the leftist sovereigntist party Québec solidaire, promised to consult Quebecers on the question of sovereignty if elected. “It doesn’t depend on Trump or any other thing that is happening in the world,” she said. 

But political analysts believe Trump’s influence will be felt throughout the electoral campaign after trade negotiations fell through last week.

Danielle Pilette, a political science professor at the Université du Québec à Montréal, compares the campaign period to the 2025 federal election, when Pierre Poilievre’s Conservatives seemed poised to win a majority government. Canadians then rallied behind Prime Minister Mark Carney and his Liberals in the face of tariff talks.

Carney also positioned himself as a defender of the French language and Quebec culture after the latest rounds of negotiations with the U.S., which Pilette believes could benefit Fréchette as the incumbent.

“We can see that public opinion is highly volatile in this unpredictable context,” she said. “In the face of that, the safe bet at federal level was the Liberals in the last election, whilst the safe bet in Quebec for this election seems to be the (governing Coalition Avenir Québec).” 

According to Université de Montréal political science professor Evelyne Brie, support for Quebec sovereignty briefly went up, but quickly diminished after Trump was elected for a second term.

“I think it was a real disadvantage for the PQ in terms of timing, because Trump seems to have had a deterrent effect on grassroots sovereignty ever since he was sworn in,” she said. “People aren’t exactly thrilled to have an additional source of uncertainty if (the PQ) might be holding a referendum.”

Like Pilette, Brie says instability typically benefits those who are already in power.

But Stéphane Paquin, the director of a group for studies and research on international affairs and Quebec, says there are significant differences between Fréchette and Carney. 

He says Carney was new on the political scene and gained credibility with his background in finance and policy. Fréchette inherited the Coalition Avenir Québec when former premier François Legault resigned after the party tanked in the polls.

“It’s easy to contrast Justin Trudeau and Mark Carney as a significant change,” said Paquin. “Christine Fréchette doesn’t have the same aura of competence as Mark Carney, and it’s going to be difficult for her to set herself apart from François Legault.”

Daniel Turp, a Université de Montréal law professor who represented both the Bloc Québécois and the PQ in Ottawa and Quebec City, agrees with Paquin. He points out that the PQ is still a favourite in the polls, with the Coalition Avenir Québec and Liberals neck-and-neck for second place.

Turp believes talks around Canadian sovereignty in the face of American threats could even benefit sovereigntist parties. 

“What’s interesting is that sovereignty is clearly becoming an important issue,” he said. “I reckon that Paul St-Pierre Plamondon could say the same thing during the campaign, that if sovereignty is so important for Canada, it’s important for Quebec too.”

Nonetheless, all four analysts agree that anything can happen on election day as polls have shown most Quebecers are open to changing their voting intention. 

“It’s going to be the most interesting campaign in recent history,” said Turp.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Aug. 28, 2026.
news.author: The Canadian Press

news.title: Despite Trump's renaming of Lake Ontario, Great Lakes endure as symbol of U.S.-Canada collaboration
news.text:
The Great Lakes, one of the largest stores of freshwater and a source of water for some 40 million people, have long symbolized how closely intertwined Canada and the U.S. are. 

U.S. President Donald Trump took a public sledgehammer to that relationship Thursday as part of his trade war with Canada, signing an executive order directing that Lake Ontario be renamed Lake America.

It's unclear whether Trump can unilaterally rename the lake, whose name predates European colonization of the Americas and has been widely recognized internationally for centuries. But the move comes amid a broader push by the Trump administration that has hindered U.S.-Canada collaboration on scientific research and restoration work in the Great Lakes.

Scientists at U.S. weather forecasting agency ordered to get clearance before talking to Canadian counterpartsThe U.S. is cutting billions from science. Canadian researchers say it's time to step up

"The way that this current administration in the United States views the environment and views science is demoralizing," said Aaron Fisk, professor at the Great Lakes Institute for Environmental Research at the University of Windsor.

"With the U.S. moving away from evidence-based decisions about the environment … that's a real concern to me because we need them to be a world leader. This really goes against their long term investment in good science," he said.

As part of its massive cuts to the federal public service, the Trump administration has made major cuts to iconic U.S. scientific agencies such as the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Environmental Protection Agency. Those cuts have, in turn, affected monitoring and research in the Great Lakes.

"The water does not respect political boundaries, and you have to manage it as a water body, as a watershed, not just as a national or state or provincial boundary," said Joel Brammeier, president and CEO of the Alliance for the Great Lakes, a U.S. non-profit that advocates for Great Lakes conservation and restoration. 

"Which is why it's always a bit painful when we see somebody out of the U.S. side challenging that collaboration. Because, honestly, the Great Lakes don't get cleaned up and they don't get protected unless the U.S. and Canada collaborate and co-operate."

Bipartisan support saves key Great Lakes program

Even amid the cuts, support for the Great Lakes has crossed political lines. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative, a two-decade-old program to restore ecosystems and clean up industrial pollution, was targeted for near-total elimination by Trump during his first administration. 

The U.S. House of Representatives voted to reauthorize the program through 2031, with nearly $500 million US in federal funding per year going to local communities in the region. The measure received both Democratic and Republican support and is now working its way through the U.S. Senate.

"There are few issues that unite political parties like the Great Lakes. The Great Lakes Restoration Initiative has been so successful in doing that," Brammeier said.

The Great Lakes region has been central to industrial growth in both the U.S. and Canada, Brammeier said, hosting major industries such as steel, chemical and aluminum manufacturing. That growth has also left widespread industrial contamination that communities across the region want cleaned up.

"Even though a lot of damage was done across a large part of the Great Lakes, in an odd way that's actually led to this near universal support for the restoration program because so many decision-makers, so many members of Congress have seen the harm in their own communities," he said.

Climate change brings new threats

Historical pollution is not the end of the Great Lakes' problems. Climate change is bringing extreme heat and shifting precipitation to the region, which researchers say requires close study on both sides of the border.

Mike Shriberg, director of the University of Michigan's Water Center, said water availability and access are emerging challenges. 

"This summer's a great example. We've had increasing drought and then increasing intensity of precipitation. So water flows have changed because of climate change," he said.

That, combined with future water demand from data centres, power generation and especially agriculture — which is expanding farther north as the climate warms — could create problems in the coming years. Shriberg also said he expects more people to move to the region from parts in the U.S. facing water shortages, particularly in the West, potentially putting further strain on the Great Lakes.

Andrew Gronewold, professor at the University of Michigan, is also thinking about future demand. "I think we're going to face some very difficult choices and questions about how Great Lakes water is used," he said from Hamilton, Ont., where he was meeting with Canadian and First Nations research partners. 

Gronewold pointed to efforts by a group of Great Lakes state governors and premiers to "future-proof" the Great Lakes compact and agreement, a set of pacts among U.S. Great Lakes states, Ontario and Quebec governing how the water is used.

"I think over the next several decades, there's going to be increased pressure from outside of the basin for that water, whether it's for agriculture or industry or other uses. That's something that we need to be paying attention to," he said.
news.summary: It's unclear whether Trump can unilaterally rename the lake, whose name predates European colonization of the Americas and has been widely recognized internationally for centuries. But the renaming belies a concerted push by the Trump administration to hold back important U.S.-Canada collaboration on scientific research and restoration work in the Great Lakes.
news.author: Inayat Singh
